# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes may fail OOD. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes on 3 held-out datasets, projecting onto a small subset of source-distribution PCs gives transfer nearly matching probes trained on the test distribution. An LLM judge scoring each PC by whether its extreme examples imply a transferable deception direction recovers part of this subset, closing the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% (Insider Trading Report) and 25% (Sandbagging). Source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferring ones encode the contrast more abstractly. Probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.

## 1 Introduction

Probes strong in-distribution can be unreliable OOD: behavioral concepts are linearly represented, yet probes learn spurious correlations, which is unacceptable for monitoring. Goal: probes that learn only generalizing features. We work in the source-domain PC basis rather than raw activations (no privileged-basis assumption) and ask which PC subset supports generalizable probes and how to identify it. Testbed: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on Roleplaying, evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging.

Contributions:
- **A small transferable subspace exists** (4.2): target-supervised greedy search finds 8–15 source PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.
- **Source- and target-side rankings fail to recover it** (4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not beat the full-representation baseline.
- **An LLM judge partially recovers it without target data** (4.5), selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast over surface patterns.

## 2 Related Work

- **Linear concept directions:** truth, honesty, emotion are represented as directions/low-dim subspaces usable for reading and intervention; single directions mediate refusal; an "assistant" axis exists. Open question: when directions capture stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations.
- **Probes and limits:** probes are used for safety signals (latent truthfulness, strategic deception). High probe accuracy does not show the model represents a property (probe may learn the task or surface correlates); probing may show only recoverable information; strong in-distribution probes generalize unevenly OOD.
- **Natural-language feature explanations:** LLMs explain neurons from high-activation examples, extended to SAE feature labeling; such descriptions have been used to select concepts to ablate during fine-tuning to reduce misalignment.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

4 deception datasets (Appendix A): Roleplaying (source); Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). GPT-4o labels honest (0), ambiguous (−1, removed), deceptive (1).

#### Language models.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual stream (prior best cross-domain AUROC layer), mean over assistant-response tokens.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Standardize with source statistics (applied to targets); PCA on source, keep top 100 PCs. Logistic regression ($\lambda=10$); subset $S$ experiments project onto $S$; baseline uses full standardized activations. Top 100 chosen since SAE decoder alignment decreases with PC index (Appendix C), aiding interpretation; not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Full-representation source probe target AUROC: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace (5-fold CV): 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869. The information is present; the source probe learns a non-generalizing direction.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Greedy selection: from empty set, add the top-100 PC most improving target AUROC; probes always fit on source projections. 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out folds, evaluate on held-out fold; stop when no gain >0.001. Average subset size: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). This is an upper bound, not an unbiased OOD estimate.

Greedy nearly matches target-trained probes on Report and Sandbagging (+0.22, +0.23 AUROC over baseline). Top-$k$-variance control ($k$ matched) matches greedy only on Confirm (easy case), far behind on the other two: PC choice matters; variance explained does not predict usefulness.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Hypotheses: transferable PCs are (i) those separating target classes well, or (ii) those the source probe already weights most. Rank PCs by standardized coefficient (|coef| × PC std) of a probe on source-PCA-projected activations trained on source ("source-PCA probe") or target ("target-PCA probe"); then train on source projected onto the top $k$. $k$ from greedy on the full target set (no CV, so numbers differ slightly from 4.2): 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging).

Both fail. Source-PCA ≈ full baseline: PCs the source probe relies on don't generalize. Target-PCA does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging: best target-separating PCs don't transfer when weighted on source. See Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

For each top-100 PC, the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples are given to an LLM, which describes positive pole, negative pole and direction, and rates generalizability 1–10 (OOD score; Appendix B). No PC scored above 6, so 6 is the maximum; PCs scoring 6 in both runs: 19.

Of the 5 PCs in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got the max score, vs 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs. Greedy-PC interpretations describe the contrast at a domain-surviving abstraction level (Appendix E).

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Probe on the 19 interp-selected PCs (max in both runs, due to judge noise), with no target data. Controls: full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, remaining 81 PCs (interp-ablated).

Interp-selected beats baseline on all 3 targets, beats the variance control by wide margins on Report and Sandbagging, and beats interp-ablated on all 3. Report: 0.706→0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy (0.929). Confirm: uninformative (baseline near ceiling; all methods except interp-ablated similar). Sandbagging: 0.606→0.662, closing 25% of the gap to greedy (0.832).

## 5 Limitations

- Single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15), single source (Roleplaying); Confirm uninformative (baseline 0.874). Generalization to other models/datasets open.
- Sandbagging gains small (25% of gap), likely reflecting it being the most OOD target; Report result is more robust.
- Fully linear pipeline (PCA + logistic regression), so a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising; nonlinear probes/other readouts untested.
- No causal validation: PC "encodings" are descriptive; high-scoring PCs not ablated at inference.

## 6 Conclusion

Robust probing requires identifying not only whether a signal is linearly accessible but where it is represented most robustly. Full-representation probes may combine general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, aiding in-distribution accuracy but hurting transfer; sparse PC subspaces may better isolate general behavioral structure. OOD probing is thus a representation-selection problem: choose a subspace preserving the intended feature and filtering spurious correlation.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes on 3 held-out datasets, projecting inputs onto a few training-distribution principal components (PCs) gives transfer nearly matching probes trained on the test distribution. An LLM judge scoring each PC on whether its extreme examples imply a transferable deception direction selects PCs that close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% (Insider Trading Report) and 25% (Sandbagging). Heavily weighted source directions encode surface features; transferring ones encode the contrast abstractly. OOD robustness is largely subspace selection.

## 1 Introduction

Probes strong in-distribution can be unreliable OOD, learning spurious correlations even though behavioral concepts are linearly represented. We work in the source-domain PCA basis (not assuming a privileged neuron basis) and ask which PC subset supports generalizable probes and how to identify it. Testbed: deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, trained on Roleplaying, evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging.

Contributions:
- **A small transferable subspace exists** (4.2): target-supervised greedy search finds 8–15 PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.
- **Source- and target-side rankings fail to recover it** (4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not beat the full-representation baseline.
- **An LLM judge partially recovers it without target data** (4.5), selecting PCs likely encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns.

Figure 1: Activations projected onto source PCA basis, PCs filtered, probes trained on selected subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

Truth, honesty, emotion, refusal and an "assistant" axis appear as linear directions usable for reading and steering, raising the question of when such directions are stable concepts versus context-dependent correlations.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Probes have been applied to latent truthfulness and strategic deception. High probe accuracy may reflect the probe learning the task or surface correlates, or information merely recoverable rather than encoded; probes strong in-distribution can generalize unevenly OOD.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

LLMs can explain neurons from high-activation examples, extended to automatic SAE feature labeling; natural-language concept identification has also been used to ablate concepts during fine-tuning to reduce misalignment.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

4 deception datasets (Appendix A): Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). GPT-4o labels: honest (0), ambiguous (-1, removed), deceptive (1).

#### Language models.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream (highest cross-domain AUROC in prior work), averaged over assistant-response tokens.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Standardize with source statistics (applied to targets); PCA on source, keep top 100 PCs. Logistic regression ($\lambda=10$); subset-$S$ probes project onto $S$; baselines use full standardized activations. Top 100 chosen because SAE decoder alignment decreases with PC index (Appendix C), aiding interpretation; not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: target AUROC for source-trained full-representation and top-100-PC probes, and target-trained top-100-PC probes (5-fold CV); 95% CIs.

Full-representation source probe: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in the 100-PC subspace: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869. So the information is present; the source probe learns a non-generalizing direction.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: AUROC for baseline, top-k PCs by variance (k matched to greedy), greedy oracle PCs; 95% CIs.

Greedy: from empty set, add the PC (of top 100) that most improves target AUROC of a probe fit on source projections. Weights always fit on source; selection uses target labels on non-held-out folds (5-fold CV), evaluated on held-out fold; stop when no gain >0.001. Mean subset sizes: 15 (Report), 8 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). This is an upper bound, not an unbiased OOD estimate.

Greedy nearly matches target-trained probes on Report and Sandbagging, +0.22 and +0.23 AUROC over baseline. Variance control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on the harder tasks: which PCs matter, and variance explained does not predict usefulness.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: AUROC for PCs ranked by source-probe weights, target-probe weights, and greedy; 95% CIs.

Hypotheses: transferable PCs (i) individually separate target classes, or (ii) are those the source probe already relies on. Rank PCs by standardized coefficient (|coef| × PC std) of a probe on source-PCA-projected activations, trained on source ('source-PCA probe') or target ('target-PCA probe'); then train on source projected onto the top $k$. $k$ from greedy on the full target set (no CV): 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging); greedy numbers thus differ slightly from 4.2.

Both fail. Source-PCA ≈ full baseline: PCs the source probe relies on don't generalize. Target-PCA does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging: target-separating PCs are not those that transfer when weighted on source. See Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

For each of the 100 PCs, the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples are given to an LLM, which describes positive pole, negative pole and direction, and rates generalizability 1–10 (OOD score; Appendix B). No PC scored above 6, so 6 is treated as maximum; PCs scoring 6 in both runs: 19.

5 PCs appeared in greedy selections for >1 target; 3 of 5 got the maximum score, vs 1 of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs. Interpretations of greedy PCs describe the contrast at a domain-surviving level of abstraction (Appendix E).

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: AUROC for interp-selected (19 PCs), baseline, top-19 by variance, and remaining 81 PCs (interp-ablated); 95% CIs.

Using the 19 interp-selected PCs (no target data), the probe beats baseline on all 3 targets, beats variance control by wide margins on Report and Sandbagging, and beats interp-ablated on all 3. Report: closes 78% of the gap from baseline (0.706) to greedy (0.929). Confirm: near ceiling, uninformative; all methods except interp-ablated similar. Sandbagging: closes 25% of the gap to greedy (0.832).

## 5 Limitations

- Single model (layer 15) and source dataset; Confirm uninformative (baseline 0.874); generality to other models/datasets open.
- Sandbagging gains small: 0.606→0.662, 25% of gap to 0.832; most OOD target. Report (0.706→0.881, 78% of gap to 0.929) is more robust.
- Fully linear pipeline, so a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising; nonlinear probes and other readout locations untested.
- No causal validation: PC "encodings" are descriptive; high-scoring PCs not ablated at inference.

## 6 Conclusion

Robust probing requires finding not just whether a signal is linearly accessible but where it is represented most robustly. Full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific cues that aid in-distribution accuracy but hurt transfer; sparse PC subspaces may isolate more general structure. OOD probing is thus a representation-selection problem: choose a subspace preserving the intended feature and filtering spurious correlation.

{"id": "q51", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Using Appendix D, why does ranking PCs by target-probe weights work well on Insider Trading Report?", "answer": "For Report, the top-13 target-separability ranking shares 4 PCs with the greedy set (PC6, PC89, PC14, PC66), giving the 0.182 Jaccard overlap. {"id": "q52", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Using the dataset descriptions and the interpretations of the source probe's top PCs, why might Insider Trading Confirm already transfer well (0.874) under the baseline?", "answer": "In Confirm, the deceptive response is a direct denial when the model is asked to confirm it used no insider information. {"id": "q53", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why must target activations be standardized with the source statistics, rather than their own, before the paper's PC-subspace probes can be applied?", "answer": "PCA is fit on the standardized source activations, and the probes are fit on source projections. {"id": "q60", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the ceiling for gap closure were the target-trained 100-PC probe (0.936) instead of the greedy oracle, would interp-selection still close more than half the gap on Insider Trading Report?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q61", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the ceiling for gap closure were the target-trained 100-PC probe (0.869) instead of the greedy oracle, would interp-selection close more than half the gap on Sandbagging?", "answer": "No. (0.662 − 0.606) / (0.869 − 0.606) = 0.056 / 0.263 ≈ 21%, far below half and even lower than the reported 25%.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Gives a computation of about 21% using 0.662, 0.606 and 0.869"]},
{"id": "q62", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to use the paper's 19 interp-selected PCs (e.g., PC62, PC57, PC86) directly as a probe subspace for a Gemma model. {"id": "q63", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to apply interp-selection with a different source dataset (for example, a customer-service lying scenario). {"id": "q64", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to extend interp-selection to PCs 101–300 in the hope of finding more transferable directions. {"id": "q65", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "To cut judge costs, a team plans to score only PC1–PC30. {"id": "q66", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A team has no labels for a new insider-trading-report setting similar to the paper's Report target. {"id": "q67", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team proposes running the LLM judge once instead of twice and keeping every PC that gets the top score. {"id": "q68", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-PCA PC sets had been close to 1 on every target, which conclusion of the paper would lose its support?", "answer": "The conclusion that the transferable subspace is not the part of representation space most discriminative on the target (Appendix D, Section 4.3). {"id": "q69", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If greedy selection had needed around 80 of the 100 PCs to reach its performance, which part of the paper's argument would be weakened?", "answer": "The claim that a small transferable subspace exists (8–15 PCs), along with the conclusion's idea that sparse PC subspaces isolate general behavioural structure. Transfer would still be possible, but the argument for a compact, interpretable transferable set would lose force.", "rubric": ["Identifies the 'small' transferable subspace claim and/or the sparse-subspace framing of the conclusion", "Explains that needing most of the PCs would contradict compactness (8–15 PCs)"]},
{"id": "q70", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the greedy oracle had stayed near the baseline on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, which of the paper's reported results would lose its meaning, in addition to the existence claim?", "answer": "The gap-closure percentages for interp-selection (78% on Report, 25% on Sandbagging). {"id": "q71", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the top-k-by-variance control (k matched to greedy) had matched greedy on Report and Sandbagging, which claim would be undermined?", "answer": "The claim that variance explained does not predict a PC's usefulness for transfer. {"id": "q72", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the judge had described PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12 as abstract, general deception strategies and scored them 6, which interpretive claim would lose its support?", "answer": "The claim that the directions a source probe weights heavily encode source-specific surface cues, while transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly. {"id": "q73", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the cross-validated greedy AUROCs (Section 4.2) had been far below the full-data greedy AUROCs, which claim would be weakened, and why?", "answer": "The claim that a transferable subspace nearly matches target-trained probes would be weakened. {"id": "q74", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that PCs the judge describes as domain-specific or surface-level cues do not transfer? {"id": "q75", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that layer 15 is the best layer at which to do PC subspace selection for deception probes? {"id": "q76", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that PC62 and PC57 carry the deny/deflect contrast in the model's computation? The PCs were never ablated during inference to verify the contrast.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the interpretations are descriptive (judge over extreme examples), with no causal ablation"]},
{"id": "q77", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that smaller PC subspaces transfer better, whatever PCs they contain? {"id": "q78", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the greedy-selected PC set is the unique transferable subspace for each target? The paper does not explore whether other subsets would transfer equally well.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that greedy finds one path-dependent set, that the sets vary across folds and data (CV vs full-data sizes), and that alternatives were not examined"]},
{"id": "q79", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the LLM judge's OOD scores are consistent from run to run? {"id": "q80", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that every PC the source probe weights heavily fails to transfer? {"id": "q83", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The 78% and 25% gap-closure figures use the greedy oracle as the ceiling. {"id": "q84", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "How robust is the list of five PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set (the yardstick used to evaluate the judge) to the particular greedy run?", "answer": "It is not guaranteed to be robust. {"id": "q85", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "PC4 received the maximum OOD score. {"id": "q86", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The full standardized activations contain every direction in the top-100 source-PC subspace, including the ones greedy finds transferable. Why does the full-representation baseline still transfer poorly?", "answer": "Having the transferable directions available does not mean the probe weights them. The probe's weights are fit to maximize separation on Roleplaying, so they load heavily on directions that are most predictive there. The paper interprets those directions (e.g., PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12) as source-specific surface cues, so the learned direction is dominated by non-generalizing cues.", "rubric": ["States that availability of the transferable directions does not ensure the source-fit probe weights them", "Reason: source fitting puts weight on directions most predictive on Roleplaying, which are source-specific surface cues (e.g., PC7/8/11/12)"]},
{"id": "q87", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Greedy selection uses target labels, yet its oracle (0.929 Report, 0.832 Sandbagging) stays below the target-trained 100-PC probe (0.936, 0.869). Why?", "answer": "Greedy uses target labels only to choose which PCs to keep. The probe weights on those PCs are still fit on Roleplaying, so they need not be the best weights for the target. The target-trained probe instead fits its weights on target data across all 100 PCs, so it can do at least as well.", "rubric": ["States that greedy still uses source-fit weights / labels only guide subset choice", "Reason: the target-trained probe optimizes weights on target data over all 100 PCs, so it can exceed any source-weighted subset"]},
{"id": "q88", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Using the label counts in Appendix A, why is AUROC a sensible metric for comparing transfer across these four datasets, rather than accuracy?", "answer": "After ambiguous labels are removed, the deceptive share differs widely: about 74% in Roleplaying (172/231), 24% in Report (61/255), 69% in Confirm (84/122) and 40% in Sandbagging (246/621). Accuracy would depend on these base rates and on a threshold set on the source. AUROC measures ranking quality and is independent of both prevalence and threshold, so comparisons stay meaningful across the shifts in class balance.", "rubric": ["States that class proportions differ greatly across datasets (e.g., ~74% deceptive in Roleplaying vs ~24% in Report)", "Reason: AUROC is threshold- and prevalence-independent, whereas accuracy would be confounded by base rates and source-set thresholds"]},
{"id": "q89", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is it sensible to test the judge against the PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set, rather than against every greedy-selected PC?", "answer": "A PC selected for only one target may reflect something specific to that target, or the greedy fit to that target's labels. A PC selected independently for two different targets is better evidence of a direction that transfers broadly. That broad transfer is exactly the out-of-domain generality the judge is asked to rate.", "rubric": ["States that multi-target PCs are better evidence of general (not target-specific) transferability", "Reason: single-target selections may reflect target-specific signal or greedy fitting, while the judge rates general OOD usefulness"]},
{"id": "q90", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Using the target-separability rankings in Appendix D, why might top-k-by-variance match greedy on Insider Trading Confirm even though it fails on the other targets?", "answer": "Confirm's class signal sits largely in high-variance source PCs. The other targets' discriminative PCs are mostly higher-index.", "rubric": ["States that Confirm's discriminative PCs are mostly low-index / high-variance", "Reason/evidence: Confirm's top target-separability PCs include PC4, PC1, PC8, PC7, which fall inside the top-7/8 variance set"]},
{"id": "q91", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "For Sandbagging, the top-14-by-variance control contains PC9, a PC greedy picked for both Report and Sandbagging. Why does it still fall far behind greedy?", "answer": "PC1–PC14 also contains most of the source probe's heavily weighted, surface-cue PCs (PC1–PC8, PC11, PC12). When weights are fit on Roleplaying, these PCs dominate the probe. The other greedy Sandbagging PCs, such as PC62, PC57 and PC86, are absent, so one transferable PC among many source-specific ones is not enough.", "rubric": ["States that the rest of PC1–PC14 is dominated by source-heavy/surface-cue PCs (PC1–8, PC11, PC12)", "Reason: source-fit weights lean on those PCs, and the other greedy PCs (e.g., PC62, PC57, PC86) are missing, so PC9 alone cannot drive transfer"]},
{"id": "q92", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Given the judge prompt in Appendix B, why would PC9 and PC81 be expected to miss the interp-selected set even though each helped transfer on two targets?", "answer": "The prompt tells the judge to give low scores (1–4) to directions that are mainly surface cues, lexical habits or task-specific phrasing. Following the rule, it scored both 3, below the maximum of 6 needed for selection.", "rubric": ["States that the judge scored them low (3) and so they were not selected", "Reason: their interpretations were surface/lexical or domain-specific cues, which the prompt explicitly instructs the judge to score low"]},
{"id": "q93", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p1", "question": "On Insider Trading Report, is the interp-selected probe's absolute AUROC gain over the full-representation baseline larger than 0.15?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q94", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p1", "question": "On Sandbagging, is the interp-selected probe's absolute AUROC gain over the full-representation baseline larger than 0.15?", "answer": "No. It rises only from 0.606 to 0.662, a gain of about 0.056 AUROC.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Supports with the gain of ~0.056 (0.662 − 0.606)"]},
{"id": "q95", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "On Insider Trading Report, does the target-trained 100-PC probe exceed the full-data greedy oracle by more than 0.02 AUROC?", "answer": "No. The two are 0.936 and 0.929, a difference of only about 0.007, so greedy essentially matches the target-trained probe.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Supports with the difference of ~0.007 (0.936 vs 0.929)"]},
{"id": "q96", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "On Sandbagging, does the target-trained 100-PC probe exceed the full-data greedy oracle by more than 0.02 AUROC?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q99", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Does the top-19-by-variance control include any of the five PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q100", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Does the top-19-by-variance control include any multi-target greedy PC that the judge gave the maximum OOD score?", "answer": "No. The max-scored multi-target PCs are PC62, PC57 and PC86, all well outside PC1–PC19.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Notes that PC62, PC57 and PC86 all have indices above 19"]},
{"id": "q101", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team has only about 20 labeled examples from their new target domain. Should they use greedy selection or interp-selection to choose PCs, based on the paper?", "answer": "Interp-selection is the safer choice. Greedy picks PCs by target AUROC and keeps adding them for gains as small as 0.001, so with about 20 labels it would largely fit noise. Even with hundreds of labels the paper treats greedy only as an optimistic upper bound. Interp-selection needs no target labels and still improved all three targets.", "rubric": ["Recommends interp-selection over greedy", "Reason: greedy selects on target AUROC with a 0.001 threshold, so with very few labels it overfits noise (and is only an upper bound), whereas interp needs no labels"]},
{"id": "q102", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team's new target closely resembles the source, and their full-representation probe already transfers well. Would the cheap top-k-by-variance control likely be enough there, based on the paper?", "answer": "Likely yes. On Confirm, the easy case with a 0.874 baseline, the top-k-by-variance control matched greedy. Variance failed only on the harder targets, Report and Sandbagging, where the source's high-variance directions do not carry the target signal.", "rubric": ["Concludes top-k variance would likely suffice on an easy, source-like target", "Reason: on Confirm (easy, high baseline) variance matched greedy, failing only on the harder targets"]},
{"id": "q103", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to use interp-selection to build a probe for sycophancy rather than deception, keeping the same source-PC pipeline. What part of the judge setup must change, and why?", "answer": "They must change the scoring criterion in the judge prompt. Left unchanged, it would select deny/deflect-style deception directions rather than sycophancy-relevant ones.", "rubric": ["States that the judge's rating criterion/prompt must be rewritten for the new behavior", "Reason: the current prompt scores usefulness for OOD deception and rewards deception strategies, so it would select deception directions"]},
{"id": "q104", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A team ran greedy selection on one labeled deception target and wants to reuse that exact PC set for a different, unlabeled deception target. Does the paper's evidence support this?", "answer": "Not well. The full-data greedy sets are largely target-specific. Report's and Confirm's sets share no PCs, and the largest overlap is only three PCs (PC62, PC57, PC9, between Report and Sandbagging). A set tuned to one target's labels mostly contains PCs that the other target's greedy search did not pick.", "rubric": ["Concludes reuse is not well supported", "Reason: greedy sets overlap little across targets (Report and Confirm share none; at most 3 shared PCs)"]},
{"id": "q105", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c6", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Inspired by the finding that source-heavy PCs are low-index, a team proposes simply dropping PC1–PC12 and probing on PC13–PC100. Does the paper directly support this rule?", "answer": "No, it is not directly tested. The evidence is only suggestive: the source probe's top PCs are mostly PC1–PC12 and are described as surface cues, and many greedy PCs are high-index. But greedy also picks low-index PCs (PC6 and PC9 for Report, PC9 for Sandbagging), and the paper never evaluates a PC13–PC100 probe. The closest test, a large leftover set (the 81 interp-ablated PCs), underperformed.", "rubric": ["Concludes the rule is not directly supported/tested by the paper", "Reason: some greedy PCs are low-index (e.g., PC6, PC9) and no PC13–100 probe was evaluated; large leftover sets like the ablated-81 did poorly"]},
{"id": "q106", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c5", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants a label-free diagnostic for whether their own source-trained deception probe relies on surface cues. Could they run the paper's judge on the PCs their probe weights most heavily, and how far could they trust the result?", "answer": "Yes, as a descriptive diagnostic. In the paper the judge scored most of the source probe's top PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12) 3–4 and described them as surface cues, consistent with the source-PCA probe transferring only at baseline. Trust should be limited, though: the scores are noisy, and PC4, also a deny/admit direction, got a 6. The interpretations are not causally validated.", "rubric": ["Concludes it is usable as a descriptive/heuristic diagnostic", "Reason: in the paper the judge flagged the source probe's top PCs as surface cues (scores 3–4), matching their poor transfer", "Condition: limited trust because judge scores are noisy (e.g., PC4 scored 6) and not causally validated"]},
{"id": "q107", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the interp-selected probe had lost to the full-representation baseline on Insider Trading Confirm only, which of the paper's statements would fail, and would the main interp-selection conclusion survive?", "answer": "The statement that interp-selection beats the baseline on all three targets would fail. The main conclusion would largely survive, because the paper treats Confirm as uninformative: its baseline is already 0.874, near the ceiling, and every method except the ablated one performs about equally there. The meaningful-improvement claim rests on Report and Sandbagging.", "rubric": ["Identifies the 'outperforms baseline on all 3 targets' statement as the one that fails", "States the main conclusion survives because Confirm is uninformative (near-ceiling baseline) and the claim rests on Report/Sandbagging"]},
{"id": "q108", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the target-PCA probe had matched greedy AUROC on all three targets while its Jaccard overlap with greedy stayed at 0.08–0.18. Would the conclusion that target-side rankings fail to recover the transferable subspace still hold?", "answer": "No. That conclusion rests mainly on performance: the target-PCA probe falls short of greedy on Confirm and goes below random on Sandbagging. If it matched greedy, a target-side ranking would recover transferable performance. The low Jaccard would then only show that different PC sets can transfer equally well, not that target ranking fails.", "rubric": ["Concludes the c4 conclusion would no longer hold", "Reason: the conclusion rests on target-PCA's performance shortfall; low overlap alone would just show multiple sets can work"]},
{"id": "q109", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the full-representation baseline on Sandbagging had been about 0.85, close to the target-trained 100-PC probe (0.869), which reported Sandbagging results would lose their meaning?", "answer": "The greedy gain of +0.23 over the baseline would be impossible, since it would push AUROC above 1. The 25% gap closure and the description of Sandbagging as the most out-of-distribution, hardest target would also no longer apply. Sandbagging would become near-ceiling and uninformative, like Confirm.", "rubric": ["Identifies the greedy +0.23 gain and/or the 25% gap-closure result as losing meaning", "Reason: a near-ceiling baseline leaves no headroom, making Sandbagging uninformative like Confirm and undercutting its 'most OOD' characterization"]},
{"id": "q110", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the source-heavy PCs PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12 had each appeared in the greedy sets of two or more targets, which interpretive claim would lose its support?", "answer": "The claim that the directions the source probe weights heavily encode source-specific surface cues, while the transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly, would lose support. Directions the judge described as surface cues would then be among the most transferable, so the contrast between the two groups would collapse.", "rubric": ["Identifies the c6 claim (source-heavy = surface cues vs transferable = abstract) as undermined", "Reason: surface-cue PCs would themselves be repeatedly selected as transferable, erasing the contrast"]},
{"id": "q111", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the greedy oracle on Insider Trading Report had been only 0.80 while interp-selection still reached 0.881, which framing in the paper would be undermined?", "answer": "Treating greedy as the upper bound or oracle, and describing interp-selection as partially recovering the transferable subspace, would both be undermined. Interp would exceed the oracle, so gap closure would be over 100% (about 0.175/0.094, roughly 186%). That would show greedy forward search had not found the best transferable subspace.", "rubric": ["Identifies the greedy-as-upper-bound/oracle framing (and 'partial recovery') as undermined", "Reason: interp would exceed the oracle, giving >100% gap closure, so greedy would not be finding the best subspace"]},
{"id": "q112", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If PC62 had appeared only in Report's greedy set and not in Sandbagging's, how would the multi-target evidence for the judge change?", "answer": "There would be four multi-target PCs (PC57, PC9, PC81, PC86), and only two of them (PC57, PC86) would have the maximum score, i.e., 2 of 4 instead of 3 of 5. This is still above the source-PCA comparison (1 of top 5) but weaker, so the support for the judge partially recovering transferable directions would be thinner.", "rubric": ["States the count becomes 2 of 4 multi-target PCs with max score (PC57, PC86)", "Concludes the evidence for c5 weakens (though still above the 1-of-5 source-PCA comparison)"]},
{"id": "q113", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that interp-selection beats a randomly chosen 19-PC subset of the top 100 PCs? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The controls are the full-representation baseline, the top-19 PCs by variance and the 81 interp-ablated PCs. No random 19-PC subset was evaluated, so the paper cannot rule out that many arbitrary small subsets of mostly higher-index PCs would also do well.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: no random-subset control was run; controls were baseline, top-19 variance and ablated-81"]},
{"id": "q114", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the existence of an 8–15 PC transferable subspace show that Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct internally represents deception in a low-dimensional subspace? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The subspace is found by a target-guided greedy search that uses target labels. The pipeline is fully linear, and the paper itself calls the existence perhaps unsurprising. No causal ablation shows that the model uses these PCs, so the result concerns probe readout, not the model's internal representation.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: selection uses target labels in a linear pipeline and there is no causal validation, so it shows a readable subspace, not how the model represents deception"]},
{"id": "q115", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the full-representation probe's poor transfer cannot be fixed by stronger regularization? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. All probes use a single regularization strength (λ = 10), and no other values were tried. The paper shows that subspace selection fixes transfer, but it does not test whether changing regularization would help.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: only λ = 10 was used; regularization strength was never varied"]},
{"id": "q116", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper establish, with a direct measure of distribution shift, that Sandbagging is the most out-of-distribution target? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper asserts that Sandbagging is the most out-of-distribution target and that the modest gain 'likely reflects' this. However, the only evidence is indirect, such as its lowest baseline AUROC (0.606) and the task description. No distance or shift statistic between Roleplaying and the targets is reported.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: the claim rests on indirect evidence (lowest baseline, task description) and is hedged ('likely'); no direct shift measure is reported"]},
{"id": "q117", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the PCs the source probe weights heavily carry no information about deception in the target domains? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Several source-heavy PCs rank high in target separability: PC4, PC1, PC8 and PC7 for Confirm, and PC5, PC6, PC4, PC1 and PC18 for Report. Some also appear in greedy sets, such as PC6 for Report and PC41 for Sandbagging. They carry target signal; the problem is how source fitting weights them.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Reason: source-heavy PCs (e.g., PC4, PC1, PC7, PC8, PC6) appear in target-separability rankings and some in greedy sets, so they do carry target information"]},
{"id": "q118", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that using SAE features instead of PCs as the selection basis would give better-transferring deception probes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. SAE features appear only in Appendix C, where the decoder alignment of each PC is used to justify keeping the top 100 PCs because they are more interpretable. No probe was trained on an SAE-feature basis, so the paper says nothing about whether such a basis would transfer better.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: SAEs are used only to justify the 100-PC cutoff via alignment; no SAE-basis probe was trained or evaluated"]}
]}

{"id": "q1", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A team recomputes the source PCA on a larger Roleplaying sample, keeping the same model, layer and pipeline. Can they keep using the paper's 19 interp-selected PC indices (e.g., PC62, PC57, PC86) without re-running the judge, and why?", "answer": "No. The interp-selected set is a list of indices into one specific Roleplaying PCA basis. Recomputing PCA on different source data changes the components and their order, so 'PC62' would no longer name the same direction. The judge has to re-score the new PCs from their own source extremes. The paper only ever uses one basis.", "rubric": ["Says the indices cannot simply be reused, or that the judge must be re-run.", "Reason: the selection refers to directions in one specific PCA basis, and recomputing PCA on new data changes or reorders the components."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The judge prompt shows each PC's extreme examples as token-by-token activations, but the PCs and probes are built from response-level vectors. For which kind of PC could this make the judge's interpretation unreliable, and why?", "answer": "The risk is a PC whose discriminative effect exists only at the level of the averaged response vector and has no salient token-level pattern. The judge infers the contrast from per-token activations. The PCA and probes, however, run on activations mean-pooled over the assistant response. The judge may therefore latch onto whatever lexical tokens stand out, rather than the response-level property the probe actually uses. The paper does not test this mismatch.", "rubric": ["Identifies PCs whose signal is diffuse or response-level rather than concentrated in particular tokens as the vulnerable case.", "Reason: the judge sees token-level activations, while PCA and probes use mean-pooled response vectors, so the judge's evidence may not match what the probe uses."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Section 4.2 calls the greedy probe an upper bound on transfer. Under what circumstance could some other source-fit PC subset beat it, and why is that possible given how greedy is run?", "answer": "A better subset could exist if it can only be reached by adding PCs that do not individually raise AUROC by more than 0.001, or by combining PCs that greedy never tries together. Greedy forward selection adds one PC at a time and stops early, and it never searches all subsets. So 'upper bound' means it is optimistic because it uses target labels, not that it is the best possible subset.", "rubric": ["Says a better subset can exist, so greedy is not a guaranteed maximum.", "Reason: greedy is one-at-a-time forward selection with a 0.001 stopping rule, not an exhaustive search; its 'upper bound' status comes from using target labels."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants a single probe that also monitors held-out Roleplaying-style conversations. Does the paper establish that the 19-PC interp-selected probe will do as well in-distribution as the full-representation probe, and what does its account suggest?", "answer": "The paper does not establish this, because it reports no held-out Roleplaying results for the interp probe. Its account suggests a possible in-distribution cost. The interp set leaves out the source probe's top-weighted PCs PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12, which scored 3–4. The Conclusion says such surface cues support high in-distribution accuracy while hurting transfer.", "rubric": ["Says the paper does not establish in-distribution parity, or says a drop is plausible.", "Reason: interp-selection drops the source-heavy surface-cue PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12) that the paper says support in-distribution accuracy, and no in-distribution numbers are reported."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Could a reader rebuild the exact full-data Sandbagging greedy set used in Section 4.3 from Appendix D's 'Greedy selection / Sandbagging' row? Use the Jaccard value to explain.", "answer": "Not exactly. The row lists 15 PCs, but Section 4.3 says k = 14. The Jaccard of 0.167 equals 4/24, which fits a 14-PC greedy set sharing four PCs (PC51, PC86, PC62, PC41) with the top-14 target ranking. With all 15 listed PCs it would be 4/25 = 0.16. So one of the listed PCs that is not shared is extra, and the paper does not say which.", "rubric": ["Says the listed row cannot be taken as the exact k = 14 set (it has 15 PCs).", "Reason: the Jaccard of 0.167 matches 4 shared PCs out of a 24-PC union (14 + 14), not 15 + 14, so one non-shared listed PC is extra."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why might no PC have scored above 6 on the judge's 1–10 OOD scale, given the judge prompt and the judge's own explanations for its top-scored PCs?", "answer": "The prompt is built to be conservative. It asks for the narrowest accurate description, low scores (1–4) for surface, brittle or context-dependent directions, and scores of 5 or more only for plausibly general strategies. Even the general-looking PCs come with caveats in the judge's explanations. PC62 is noisy because honest speakers also deny, PC57 is brittle and lexical, and PC86 gives false positives from politeness or privacy. Those caveats hold the scores down to the low end of the 5+ band.", "rubric": ["Attributes the 6 ceiling to the prompt's conservative scoring instructions (narrowest description, 1–4 for brittle or surface cues, 5+ only for general strategies).", "Notes that even the best PCs' explanations list noise or brittleness caveats, which keep their scores moderate."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "PC4 ranks in the top-k target-separability list for all three targets, got the maximum OOD score, and is a top-5 source-probe PC. Why does it appear in none of the full-data greedy sets?", "answer": "Greedy keeps PCs that help transfer when their weights are fit on source data, not PCs that separate the target when weighted on target data. PC4's source-side contrast leans on surface cues such as explicit 'Yes'/'No' turns and defensive phrasing. Its source-fit weight therefore does not carry over well. This is the paper's general finding that the best target-separating PCs are not the ones that keep transferring when weighted using source data.", "rubric": ["States that target separability does not imply transfer once the weights are fit on source data.", "Links this to PC4 relying on source surface cues (explicit Yes/No, defensive phrasing), so its source-fit weight does not carry over."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The top-19-by-variance control contains three Report greedy PCs (PC6, PC9, PC14) and the max-scored PC4, yet it loses badly to interp-selection on Insider Trading Report. Why?", "answer": "PC1–PC19 also include PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12, along with PC1–PC3 and PC5. These are the PCs the source probe weights most heavily, and the judge describes the first four as surface cues. A probe fit on source data in this subspace leans on them again. The source-PCA probe built on such PCs transfers only about as well as the baseline, so having a few useful PCs present does not rescue transfer.", "rubric": ["Points out that the variance-19 set also contains the source-heavy surface-cue PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, and/or PC1–PC5).", "Reason: a source-fit probe leans on those PCs, as shown by the source-PCA probe transferring about as well as the baseline, which swamps the useful PCs."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the Limitations section call the existence of a transferable subspace 'perhaps unsurprising', given the Section 4.1 results?", "answer": "In the same 100-PC space, a target-trained linear probe reaches 0.936, 0.950 and 0.869. So a good linear separator for each target already exists there. Greedy uses target labels to choose which coordinates the source-fit probe may use. In a fully linear pipeline, finding a subset where the source-fit weights roughly line up with that separator is a modest requirement.", "rubric": ["Notes that target-trained linear probes in the same 100-PC space already separate the targets well (0.87–0.95).", "Reason: greedy only needs to use target labels to pick coordinates where the source-fit linear weights approximate that separator, which is easy in a linear pipeline."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does greedy selection stop at 8–15 PCs rather than growing toward all 100, even though each added PC gives the probe more information?", "answer": "Each added PC also gives the source-fit probe more room to put weight on directions that do not generalize. The limiting case, training on everything, is the poorly transferring baseline. After the first few transferable PCs, further additions stop raising target AUROC by more than 0.001, so greedy stops.", "rubric": ["States that adding more PCs lets the source-fit probe re-weight toward non-generalizing directions, so target AUROC stops improving.", "Supports this with the poor transfer of the full-representation baseline (the 'use everything' limit) together with the 0.001 stopping rule."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Sandbagging has more evaluation examples than Insider Trading Report (621 vs 255 after removing ambiguous labels). Why does the paper still treat the Report interp result as the more robust one?", "answer": "Robustness here is about effect size, not sample size. On Report, interp-selection gains 0.175 AUROC (0.706 to 0.881) and closes 78% of the gap. On Sandbagging it gains only 0.056 (0.606 to 0.662) and closes 25%. A more precisely measured small effect is still a small effect.", "rubric": ["Says the Report result is more robust because its gain is much larger (about 0.175 vs 0.056, or 78% vs 25% gap closure).", "Notes that Sandbagging's larger sample gives a more precise estimate but does not make a small gain larger or more convincing."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Does the full-data greedy set for Sandbagging (Appendix D) contain any PC from the source-probe-weight list?", "answer": "Yes. PC41 is on the source-probe-weight list (14th) and also in the Sandbagging greedy set.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Names PC41 as the shared PC."]},

{"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p3", "question": "On Insider Trading Report, do the full-data greedy set and the top-13 target-separability ranking share more than one PC?", "answer": "Yes, four: PC6, PC89, PC14 and PC66. {"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p3", "question": "On Insider Trading Confirm, do the full-data greedy set and the top-7 target-separability ranking share more than one PC?", "answer": "No, only PC53. {"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "Does the Insider Trading Report top-13 target-separability ranking include any of the five PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set?", "answer": "No. None of PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81 or PC86 is in Report's top-13. {"id": "q21", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": "p5", "question": "Does any of PC6–PC10 appear in any target's full-data greedy set?", "answer": "Yes.
