# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes are a standard means of reading behaviors and concepts from language model activations, but their out-of-distribution behavior is unreliable. We study source-to-target transfer of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes across 3 held-out datasets and find that projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) of the source activation distribution yields cross-domain AUROC close to that of probes fit directly on the target distribution. A subset of these PCs is recoverable from PC interpretations alone: an LLM judge scores each PC from its most/least activating source examples for a transferable deception contrast, and a probe on the highest-scoring PCs closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Heavily weighted source-probe directions are judged to track surface features of the source, whereas oracle-selected directions are described in more abstract terms. We interpret these results in terms of subspace selection.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are cheap, widely used readouts of model internals (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019), but strong in-distribution performance does not guarantee out-of-distribution reliability (Kirch et al., 2026). Key behavioral concepts are linearly represented (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), so capacity is not the obstacle; nonetheless probes pick up spurious correlates in practice (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), which is incompatible with probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions.

We work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than the residual-stream basis, which we do not treat as privileged. PC choice is known to matter: Mu et al. (2018) improve embeddings by removing top PCs, and Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. Our question is which PC subsets support generalizable probe training and how they can be identified.

The testbed is deception probing on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024): a single source dataset (Roleplaying) and 3 held-out targets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging) (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Contributions:

•

A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2).
Target-supervised greedy search over source PCs returns 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.

•

Source-side and target-side rankings both fail to
recover the subspace
(Section 4.3). Rankings by source- or target-probe weights do not outperform the full-representation baseline.

•

An LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without
target data (Section 4.5).
Judge-scored PC selection transfers better than baseline and variance-matched controls.

Figure 1: Overview of PC-based subspace selection for OOD deception probing. Activations are projected onto the source-domain PCA basis, candidate PC directions are filtered, and probes are trained on the selected low-dimensional subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

Marks and Tegmark (2024) report cross-dataset linear structure in true/false representations; Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and relate it to probing and steering; Zou et al. (2025) treat honesty, emotion and similar properties as population-level directions available for reading and intervention. Arditi et al. (2024) show refusal is mediated by a single direction, and Lu et al. (2026) identify an “assistant” axis. These results support linear structure for mechanistic understanding and activation-space intervention, while leaving open when such directions capture stable concepts versus context-dependent correlates.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Probes have long been used to analyze represented information (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019) and have more recently been applied to safety-relevant signals, including unsupervised latent truthfulness (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Hewitt and Liang (2019) note that probe accuracy alone does not establish that the model represents a property, since the probe may learn the task or exploit surface correlates; Ravichander et al. (2021) question whether probing shows encoded versus merely recoverable information. Probes strong in-distribution can also generalize unevenly (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini), which motivates evaluating whether safety probes track robust internal signals or dataset artifacts.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

Bills et al. (2023) generate LLM explanations of neurons from high-activation examples; the approach has been extended to automatic labeling of sparse autoencoder features ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)). Casademunt et al. (2025) use automated natural-language interpretation to identify concepts and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

We use 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging; Appendix A). Roleplaying is the source; the other 3 are targets. GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) labels each response honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are discarded.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the layer with highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis, mean-pooled over assistant-response tokens.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Activations are z-scored with source statistics (applied unchanged to targets). PCA is fit on scaled source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic regression ( $\lambda=10$ ); subset-$S$ probes are trained and evaluated on projections onto $S$, baselines on the full standardized activations.

The cutoff at 100 is motivated by SAE decoder alignment (Bricken et al., 2023) decreasing with PC index (Appendix C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable and comparable with interpretability-driven selection. This is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better; Section 4.1 addresses whether the 100-PC subspace is sufficient on each target.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Error bars: 95% CIs

Source-trained full-representation probes reach 0.874 AUROC on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging (Figure 2). Target-trained probes within the 100-PC subspace (5-fold CV) reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869. The deficit of source-trained probes is therefore attributable to the direction they select within the subspace.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the full-representation baseline (blue), top-k PCs by variance (teal, k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Greedy oracle selection grows $S$ from $\emptyset$, at each step adding the PC among the top 100 that maximizes target AUROC of a logistic probe fit on source projections onto $S$, and halts when no candidate improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Weights are always fit on source data; selection is run on the non-held-out folds of 5-fold target CV and scored on the held-out fold. Mean subset sizes are 15 PCs (Insider Trading Report), 8 (Insider Trading Confirm), and 14 (Sandbagging). Because selection consumes target labels, greedy is an upper bound rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. The control takes the top $k$ PCs by variance with $k$ matched to greedy (Figure 3).

Greedy approaches target-trained performance on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, improving on baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC respectively. Variance-ranked top-$k$ matches greedy only on Insider Trading Confirm and falls far behind on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging; explained variance does not predict utility.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Probe AUROC across the three targets for three PC-selection rules: ranking by source-probe weights (red), by target-probe weights (pink), and greedy oracle selection (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We test 2 hypotheses for the content of the greedy subset: (i) it consists of the PCs that individually separate the target classes, accessible to greedy via its target labels; (ii) it consists of the PCs the source probe already weights most heavily, recovered in compact form.

PCs are ranked by standardized coefficient $|w_j|\,\sigma_j$ from a probe on source-PCA projections: the ‘source-PCA probe’ is fit on source data, the ‘target-PCA probe’ on target data. In both cases a fresh probe is then trained on source data projected onto the top $k$ PCs of the respective ranking. $k$ is fixed by running greedy once on the full target set (no CV): $k=13$ for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging; greedy numbers here therefore differ slightly from Section 4.2 (Figure 4).

The source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. The target-PCA probe does well on Insider Trading Report, worse than greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, and below chance on Sandbagging. Further set comparisons are in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Following Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025), for each of the top 100 source PCs we take the 8 most and 8 least PC-activating source examples and prompt an LLM to describe the positive pole, negative pole, and shared direction, and to rate OOD usefulness on a 1–10 scale (OOD score; prompt and model in Appendix B). No PC exceeded 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed OOD score; PCs at this maximum in both runs number 19.

Of the 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for more than one target, 3 received the maximum OOD score, against 1 of the top 5 PCs by source-PCA-probe weight. Judge descriptions of greedy-selected PCs are pitched at a level of abstraction that is not tied to source phrasing (Appendix E).

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the interp-selected subspace (red; 19 PCs) versus three controls: full-representation baseline (blue), top-19 PCs by variance (teal), and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs (brown). Error bars: 95% CIs.

The probe subspace is the set of PCs at the maximum OOD score in both of two judge runs (to mitigate judge noise), giving 19 interp-selected PCs and no use of target data. Controls are the interp-ablated complement (the 81 remaining PCs) and the top 19 source PCs by variance (Figure 5).

The interp-selected probe beats baseline on all 3 targets, beats the variance control by wide margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, and beats the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. On Insider Trading Report it closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and greedy (0.929). On Insider Trading Confirm, baseline transfer is near ceiling and all methods other than interp-ablated perform comparably, so this target is uninformative. On Sandbagging it closes 25% of the gap to greedy (0.832).

## 5 Limitations

Our strongest claims are narrow.

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Insider Trading Confirm is uninformative, with baseline transfer already at 0.874. Generalization to other model families or datasets is left open.

Sandbagging margins are small.
Interpretability selection raises Sandbagging AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound (0.832); Sandbagging is also the most out-of-distribution target, which plausibly accounts for the modest gain. Insider Trading Report (0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929) is the more robust result.

Linear pipeline. The pipeline (PCA projection followed by logistic regression) is fully linear, so the existence of a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising. Extension to nonlinear probes or other readout locations is open.

No causal validation.
Claims about what a PC “encodes” rest on top-activating examples and the judge’s verbalization and are descriptive. We have not ablated high-scoring PCs at inference to verify the contrast they appear to carry.

## 6 Conclusion

In probe-based deception monitoring, a small subset of source-domain principal components (PCs) supports cross-domain transfer close to target-trained probes, and this subset is not recovered by source-side or target-side separability. A target-free LLM-judge interpretability score over each PC’s top-activating examples partially recovers it.

Robust probing then depends not only on whether a behavioral signal is linearly accessible but on where in activation space it is most robustly represented. Full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues that sustain in-distribution accuracy at the cost of transfer, whereas sparse PC subspaces may better isolate general behavioral structure. OOD probing is accordingly a representation-selection problem: fitting a classifier and choosing a subspace that retains the intended feature while excluding spurious correlation.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes can be used to detect behaviors and concepts inside language model activations, but may fail to transfer to out-of-distribution examples. We study the generalization of deception probes trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Rather than working in the raw activation basis, we analyze probes in the basis of principal components (PCs) of the training distribution of activations. This basis gives a common coordinate system for asking which directions a source probe relies on and how those directions behave under distribution shift. Within this framework we describe several complementary ways of choosing PC subsets: a target-supervised greedy search, rankings based on source-probe and target-probe weights, and a target-free procedure in which an LLM judge scores each PC on whether its most and least activating examples suggest a transferable deception direction. We report baseline cross-domain transfer for full-representation probes, which ranges from reasonable to near chance depending on the target. We then discuss what each selection procedure can and cannot reveal about where deception-relevant structure lives in activation space. Broadly, the framework treats probe robustness as a question about the geometry of the representation the probe is allowed to use, and offers a vocabulary and set of tools for studying it.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are standard tooling for reading information from language model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019).
They are cheap to train and expose some semantically meaningful information in an otherwise opaque representation space.
However, probes that look strong in-distribution are sometimes unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026). Existing work shows that key behavioral concepts are linearly represented in model activations (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), so probes should in principle be able to detect these concepts, yet in practice they appear to pick up spurious correlations (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). For probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions this is a serious problem, and it sets a clear challenge:
how can we build probes that only learn generalizing features?

To approach this question, we work in the basis of source-domain principal components (PCs) rather than raw activations. This avoids assuming that the model’s latent dimensions form a privileged basis. Principal components are a simple, data-driven way to study structure in representation spaces, and prior work suggests that the choice of PCs matters. Mu et al. (2018) show that removing the top PCs of an embedding space improves downstream performance, and Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. Our investigation therefore centers on two questions: how should one reason about which principal components a probe ought to use, and what tools are available for choosing among them?

Our testbed is deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024).
We train them on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate them on 3 held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging) (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).
Working in the source-domain PCA basis, we lay out strategies for selecting a subset of training dimensions, with the aim of reducing reliance on spurious correlations and improving transfer to target domains.

This work contributes the following:

•

A PCA-based framing of probe transfer (Section 3). We describe a pipeline that standardizes activations with source statistics, projects them onto a fixed source PCA basis, and trains probes on chosen subsets of components. Transfer questions then become questions about which components are used.

•

A family of selection procedures
(Sections 4.2–4.3). We describe a target-supervised greedy search, which serves as an analysis tool, and rankings based on source-probe and target-probe weights. Each corresponds to a distinct hypothesis about what makes a direction transferable.

•

A target-free, interpretability-driven selection method (Sections 4.4–4.5).
We describe how an LLM judge can interpret each PC from its extreme activating examples and score whether it seems to encode a general behavioral contrast rather than a surface pattern.

Figure 1: Overview of PC-based subspace selection for OOD deception probing. Activations are projected onto the source-domain PCA basis, candidate PC directions are filtered, and probes are trained on the selected low-dimensional subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

A related line of work asks whether high-level behavioral or semantic properties are represented as directions or low-dimensional subspaces in activation space. Marks and Tegmark (2024) report linear structure in true/false representations across datasets. Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and connect it to both probing and steering. Zou et al. (2025) model high-level properties such as honesty and emotion as population-level directions that can be read from and intervened on in model activations.

This perspective has also been used to explain and control model behavior. Arditi et al. (2024) show that a single direction can mediate refusal behavior, which suggests that some high-level behaviors may be localized in simple linear features. Lu et al. (2026) similarly identify an “assistant” axis corresponding to assistant-like behavior. These works suggest that linear structure can support both mechanistic understanding and activation-space interventions. They also raise the question of when such directions capture stable concepts and when they capture context-dependent correlations. A direction found on one dataset may combine a concept with the idiosyncrasies of how that dataset expresses it, and separating the two is part of the motivation for our framing.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Linear and lightweight probes have a long history in interpretability as tools for analyzing what information neural networks represent (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Recent work has applied such probes to safety-relevant signals in LLM activations, including latent truthfulness without direct supervision (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

Methodological skepticism is central to the probing literature. Hewitt and Liang (2019) argue that high probe accuracy alone does not show that a model already represents the target property, since the probe may itself learn the task or exploit surface-level correlates. Ravichander et al. (2021) similarly question whether probing reliably establishes what information is encoded, as opposed to merely recoverable. Recent work also finds that probes with strong in-distribution performance can generalize unevenly out of distribution (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini). These concerns motivate careful evaluation of whether safety probes identify robust internal signals or dataset-specific artifacts. They also motivate methods that constrain which parts of the representation a probe is allowed to use, and not only how well it fits.

#### Dimensionality reduction and representation geometry.

Principal component analysis has long been used to summarize and post-process learned representations. Beyond the embedding post-processing of Mu et al. (2018), PCA-based projections appear in work on representation anisotropy, in linear concept erasure, and as baselines for probing and steering. A recurring observation is that the highest-variance directions of a representation space are not necessarily the most semantically informative. Dominant components may instead reflect frequency effects, formatting, or other global properties of the data. This suggests that variance and usefulness are distinct notions, and that a basis such as PCA is most valuable as a coordinate system in which selection can be studied, not as a ranking of importance.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

Another approach interprets internal representations by assigning natural-language descriptions to neurons or learned features. Bills et al. (2023) introduced the use of LLMs to generate explanations of neurons from high-activation examples. This approach has since been extended to automatic labeling of features in sparse autoencoders (Paulo et al., 2025; Bricken et al., 2023), which allows large-scale interpretation of learned feature dictionaries.

Recent work has also asked whether natural-language feature descriptions can be used for intervention as well as interpretation. For example, Casademunt et al. (2025) identify concepts through automated natural-language interpretation and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior. Our interpretability-driven selection follows this line by using descriptions to decide which directions a probe may rely on.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

Following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025), we use 4 of their deception detection datasets (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging), described in Appendix A.

Roleplaying is our source domain and the other 3 are target test sets. Each response is labeled as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) by GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024), and we remove ambiguous responses for our experiments. The targets differ from the source in different ways. The Insider Trading datasets embed deception in an agentic financial setting, while Sandbagging concerns strategic underperformance rather than verbal misstatement. This gives a range of distribution shifts that a single source probe has to cope with.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the layer with the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. To extract activations, we pass each prompt through the model and average token activations over the assistant’s response only.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

We standardize source activations to zero mean and unit variance, then apply the same source statistics to standardize all target activations. We run PCA on the scaled source activations and keep the top 100 PCs. All probes are logistic regression classifiers ( $\lambda=10$ ). For experiments using a subset $S$ of these 100 PCs, activations are projected onto $S$ before training and evaluation. The baseline probes train directly on the full standardized activations.

We use the top 100 PCs because alignment with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index (Appendix C). Lower-index PCs are therefore more amenable to natural-language interpretation, which makes them a natural candidate pool for interpretability-driven selection methods. This is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better. It is a practical choice that keeps every candidate direction within reach of the interpretation procedure in Section 4.4.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We first test how well probes trained on the full source representations transfer to each target. The results are shown in Figure 2.
Insider Trading Confirm transfers reasonably well (0.874 AUROC) and Insider Trading Report moderately (0.706 AUROC), while Sandbagging transfers poorly (0.606 AUROC).

This spread reflects the different kinds of shift involved. Insider Trading Confirm asks the model for an explicit denial after concealment, which is close to the question-and-answer format of Roleplaying. Insider Trading Report requires the model to frame a summary selectively. Sandbagging, the most distant target, involves deliberately degraded task performance rather than a direct verbal lie. A probe whose decision boundary is shaped by the conversational style of Roleplaying will plausibly track the targets that share that style more closely.

Restricting the source probe to the top-100 PC projection changes the picture little, which is expected given that the projection is fixed by source statistics alone. The baseline therefore frames the central question for the rest of the paper: given a fixed source basis, how might one decide which of its directions a probe should be permitted to use?

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Schematic of the greedy PC-selection procedure: at each step, candidate PCs are added to the current subset, a probe is fit on source data, and the candidate is scored on held-out target folds.

A natural way to study transfer in the PC basis is to ask directly which components help a source-trained probe on a given target.
We describe a greedy algorithm for PC selection for this purpose.
Starting from an empty set, we add PCs from the source basis one at a time.
At each step, we search over the top 100 PCs and add the one that most improves AUROC on the target.
To evaluate each candidate, we project source activations onto the current subset and train a logistic regression probe on those projections.

Probe weights are always fit on source data, while the choice of PC subsets is guided by performance on labeled examples from the target dataset.
We use 5-fold cross-validation over the target dataset: greedy PC selection is performed on the non-held-out target folds, and the selected source-trained probe is evaluated on the held-out target fold. The search stops when no candidate PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001.

This procedure is best understood as an analysis instrument, not a deployable method. Because subset selection uses target examples, it measures how far careful selection could push a source-trained probe. It is not an unbiased estimate of out-of-distribution performance. Its value lies in separating two roles that are usually entangled in a probe: the data used to fit weights and the data used to choose the space in which those weights live.

A natural reference point for any subset-selection rule is to take the top $k$ PCs by variance, where $k$ matches the size of the subset under comparison. Variance-based truncation is the default in most PCA pipelines. Comparing against it tests whether a selection rule does anything beyond simple dimensionality reduction. If variance alone determined which directions carry transferable information, any principled selection procedure would reduce to this baseline.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Schematic of the two weight-based PC rankings: by source-probe standardized weights and by target-probe standardized weights.

If some subsets of PCs transfer better than others, what property of those PCs would make them transferable, and could that property be detected from the source side alone?
We consider 2 simple hypotheses.
The first is that transferable PCs are simply those that separate the target classes well by themselves across the test set, which a target-guided search would naturally find.
The second is that they are the PCs the source probe already leans on most heavily, in which case any compact selection would just be a concentrated form of the source signal.

We formalize these hypotheses as 2 rankings of PCs. Both are based on the standardized coefficient, the absolute value of each probe coefficient multiplied by the standard deviation of the corresponding PC.

The ‘source-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on source data. The ‘target-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on target data. In both cases the activations are projected onto the source-PCA basis, and the final probes are trained on source data projected onto the top $k$ PCs of the respective ranking.
Each ranking thus produces a candidate subspace that can be compared against the full-representation baseline and against variance-based truncation.

The two hypotheses make different predictions. Under the second hypothesis, ranking by source-probe weight is enough, and no target information is needed. Under the first, target separability is the key property, but it requires labeled target data. Neither hypothesis says anything about the abstraction level of what a direction encodes. A heavily weighted source direction might capture deception itself, or a lexical habit that happens to co-occur with deception in Roleplaying. This ambiguity motivates the interpretability-based analysis in the next two sections. Representative PCs favored by the source-probe ranking are listed in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Weight-based rankings treat each PC as an anonymous axis. A complementary view asks whether individual PCs correspond to anything human-interpretable, and whether interpretation can say something about likely transfer that weights alone cannot.
To study this, we adopt the interpretability method of Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025).

For each of the top 100 source PCs, we find the 8 most and 8 least PC-activating examples from the source data. We then prompt an LLM to generate a natural-language description of the positive pole, the negative pole, and the PC direction as a whole.
The LLM judge also rates the generalizability of each direction on a 1–10 scale (OOD score). The full judge prompt and model details are given in Appendix B.
The prompt explicitly asks for low scores on directions dominated by surface cues, lexical habits, or task-specific phrasing, and reserves higher scores for directions plausibly tied to a general deception-relevant strategy.

This procedure turns each PC into an object that can be inspected and argued about. Descriptions differ in kind as well as in content. Some describe a pragmatic strategy, such as denying or deflecting versus volunteering details. Others describe stylistic register, domain vocabulary, or the presence of particular tokens such as an explicit “No” or “Yes”. Example judge outputs for PCs heavily weighted by the source probe are given in Appendix E. The scores are coarse and the descriptions are necessarily partial, since 16 examples can only hint at what a 4096-dimensional direction encodes. Still, they offer a source-only signal that is orthogonal to probe weights.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Schematic of interp-based selection and its controls: the interp-selected subspace, the full-representation baseline, the top PCs by variance, and the complement of the interp-selected PCs.

Interpretation suggests a selection rule that uses no target data: keep the PCs whose descriptions the judge considers most likely to generalize.
In practice, judge scores cluster in the middle of the scale, and we treat the maximum observed OOD score as the selection threshold.
Because LLM judge scores are noisy, we run the scoring twice and keep only PCs that receive the maximum score in both runs, which yields 19 interp-selected PCs.

Evaluating such a rule requires controls that separate the effect of which PCs are chosen from the effect of choosing fewer of them. We consider two. The first is the top 19 source PCs by variance, which matches dimensionality without using interpretation. The second is the complement of the selected set, the 81 PCs not chosen, which tests whether the judge is concentrating or merely removing signal. Insider Trading Confirm offers limited headroom for comparison, since its baseline already transfers well. Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging are the more demanding settings for any selection method.

The appeal of this approach is that it shifts part of the burden of generalization from data to judgment. Instead of requiring labeled examples from every deployment distribution, it asks a question that can be answered on the source domain alone: does this direction describe the behavior we care about, or the way one dataset happens to express it? How reliably a language model can answer that question is itself an empirical matter, and it depends on the quality of the extreme-example summaries, the calibration of the judge, and the consistency of its ratings across runs.

## 5 Limitations

Our framework is intentionally narrow, and there are several limitations the reader should keep in mind.

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and a single source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Insider Trading Confirm also provides limited room for comparison, since baseline transfer already reaches 0.874. Whether our framing extends to other model families, layers, or source datasets is an open question we leave to future work.

Difficult targets.
Sandbagging is the most out-of-distribution target, and its baseline transfer (0.606) is close to chance. Deception expressed through degraded task performance may engage representations quite different from those exercised by conversational lying. Any method that relies on a source-domain basis may therefore have limited reach on such targets.

Linear pipeline. Our probe pipeline is fully linear (PCA projection followed by logistic regression). Linearity makes the subspace framing natural and keeps the analysis tractable, but it may not reflect how nonlinear probes or other readout locations behave.

Judge reliability.
The interpretability-driven method depends on an LLM judge whose scores are coarse, cluster in a narrow range, and vary between runs. Requiring agreement across two runs reduces this noise but does not remove it. The judge also sees only a small number of extreme examples per direction.

No causal validation.
Our descriptions of what each PC “encodes” come from top-activating examples and an LLM judge’s verbalization of the contrast.
These are descriptive claims, not causal ones. We have not ablated PCs during inference to verify that they carry the contrast they appear to encode.

## 6 Conclusion

We have described a framework for studying deception-probe transfer in the basis of source-domain principal components. Baseline transfer from Roleplaying varies considerably across targets, from reasonable on Insider Trading Confirm to near chance on Sandbagging. We outlined a set of selection procedures that make different assumptions about what makes a direction transferable: target-guided greedy search, weight-based rankings, and an interpretability score produced by an LLM judge without access to target data.

A broader point is that robust probing involves more than establishing that a behavioral signal is linearly accessible. It also requires thinking about where in activation space a probe draws that signal from. Linear probes trained over full representations may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, and such mixtures can support high in-distribution accuracy while being fragile under shift. Restricting probes to interpretable, deliberately chosen directions is one way to make that mixture visible and open to scrutiny. We hope the tools described here are useful for understanding when probes can be trusted beyond the data they were trained on.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes can be used to detect behaviors and concepts inside language model activations, but may fail to transfer to out-of-distribution examples. We study Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on one source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Projecting inputs onto a small subset of source-domain principal components (PCs), chosen by a target-guided greedy search, yields source-trained probes whose cross-domain AUROC nearly matches that of probes trained directly on the test distribution. Neither source-probe nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover this subset. We have an LLM judge score each PC on whether its most and least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, and we then probe on the highest-scoring PCs. This uses no target data and closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are standard tooling for reading information from language model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). They are cheap to train and expose semantically meaningful information in an otherwise opaque representation space. Probes that are strong in-distribution can, however, be unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026). Key behavioral concepts are linearly represented in model activations (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), so probes have the capacity to detect them. In practice, though, probes pick up spurious correlations (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). This is a problem for probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions.

We work in the basis of source-domain principal components (PCs) rather than raw activations, so we do not assume that the model's latent dimensions form a privileged basis. Prior work suggests that the choice of PCs matters. Mu et al. (2018) find that removing the top PCs of an embedding space improves downstream performance. Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. We therefore ask which subset of PCs supports generalizable probe training, and how that subset can be identified.

Our testbed is deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We train on Roleplaying and evaluate on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

Our contributions are as follows.

•

A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2). A target-supervised greedy search over source PCs selects 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.

•

Source-side and target-side rankings both fail to recover the subspace (Section 4.3). Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not give a basis that transfers better than the full-representation baseline.

•

An LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data (Section 4.5). We select PCs using judge scores assigned to natural-language interpretations of each PC.

Figure 1: Overview of PC-based subspace selection for OOD deception probing. Activations are projected onto the source-domain PCA basis, candidate PC directions are filtered, and probes are trained on the selected low-dimensional subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

Marks and Tegmark (2024) report linear structure in true/false representations across datasets. Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and connect it to both probing and steering. Zou et al. (2025) model honesty and emotion as population-level directions that can be read from and intervened on. Arditi et al. (2024) show that a single direction mediates refusal. Lu et al. (2026) identify an "assistant" axis corresponding to assistant-like behavior. This line of work leaves open when such directions capture stable concepts and when they capture context-dependent correlations.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Probes have long been used to analyze what information networks represent (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). More recently they have been applied to latent truthfulness without direct supervision (Burns et al., 2024) and to strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Hewitt and Liang (2019) argue that high probe accuracy does not show that the model represents a property, because the probe may learn the task itself or exploit surface correlates. Ravichander et al. (2021) question whether probing establishes what is encoded or only what is recoverable. Probes with strong in-distribution performance can generalize unevenly out of distribution (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini).

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

Bills et al. (2023) use LLMs to explain neurons from high-activation examples. This approach was later extended to sparse autoencoder features ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)). Casademunt et al. (2025) identify concepts through automated natural-language interpretation and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

We use 4 deception detection datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Appendix A). Roleplaying is the source domain and the other 3 are targets. GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) labels each response as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1). We remove ambiguous responses.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), which was the layer with the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. For each prompt, we average token activations over the assistant's response only.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Target activations are standardized with the same source statistics. We fit PCA on the scaled source activations and keep the top 100 PCs. All probes are logistic regression ( $\lambda=10$ ) evaluated by target AUROC. For a subset $S$ of the 100 PCs, activations are projected onto $S$ before training and evaluation. Baseline probes train on the full standardized activations.

We restrict to the top 100 PCs because alignment with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index (Appendix C). This makes lower-index PCs easier to interpret in natural language and comparable with interpretability-driven selection. We do not claim that low-index PCs generalize better.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Error bars: 95% CIs

Source-trained probes on the full representations reach 0.874 AUROC on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging (Figure 2). Probes trained on target data within the top-100 source PC subspace, using 5-fold cross-validation, reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the full-representation baseline (blue), top-k PCs by variance (teal, k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

The greedy oracle starts from the empty set. At each step it adds whichever of the top 100 PCs most improves the target AUROC of a logistic regression probe fit on source activations projected onto the current subset. Probe weights are always fit on source data, while subset choice uses labeled target examples. Under 5-fold cross-validation over the target, selection runs on the non-held-out folds and the selected source-trained probe is scored on the held-out fold. Search stops when no candidate improves AUROC by more than 0.001. It converges, on average, to 15 PCs for Insider Trading Report, 8 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Because selection uses target examples, greedy is an upper bound on transfer, not an unbiased OOD estimate. As a control, we take the top $k$ PCs by variance, with $k$ matched to the greedy count (Figure 3).

Greedy approaches the target-trained probe on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, exceeding the baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC respectively. The variance control matches greedy only on Insider Trading Confirm and falls far behind on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Probe AUROC across the three targets for three PC-selection rules: ranking by source-probe weights (red), by target-probe weights (pink), and greedy oracle selection (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We test two hypotheses about the greedy subset. Under the first, the selected PCs are those that separate target classes well, and greedy finds them because it has target access. Under the second, they are the PCs the source probe already weights most heavily, recovered in compact form.

We rank PCs by standardized coefficient, defined as the absolute value of a probe coefficient times the standard deviation of the corresponding PC. The coefficients come from probes on activations projected onto the source-PCA basis. The "source-PCA probe" ranking uses a probe fit on source data. The "target-PCA probe" ranking uses a probe fit on target data. For each ranking, we fit a probe on source data projected onto that ranking's top $k$ PCs and evaluate it on the target.

To fix $k$, we run greedy once on the full target dataset rather than per fold. This gives $k=13$ for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. The greedy numbers here therefore differ slightly from the CV numbers in Section 4.2 (Figure 4).

The source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. The target-PCA probe does well on Insider Trading Report, is worse than greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, and falls below chance on Sandbagging. PC set comparisons are given in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Following Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025), we take the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples for each of the top 100 source PCs. An LLM then describes the positive pole, the negative pole, and the shared direction, and rates the direction's usefulness for out-of-distribution deception detection on a 1–10 scale (OOD score; prompt and model in Appendix B). No PC scored above 6, so 6 is the maximum observed OOD score. We run scoring twice. The 19 PCs that reach this maximum in both runs form the interp-selected set.

Five PCs appear in the greedy selections of more than one target, and 3 of these 5 receive the maximum OOD score. Of the top 5 PCs by source-PCA probe weight, 1 receives the maximum OOD score. Appendix E gives per-PC breakdowns.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the interp-selected subspace (red; 19 PCs) versus three controls: full-representation baseline (blue), top-19 PCs by variance (teal), and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs (brown). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We train source probes on the 19 interp-selected PCs, using no target data. We compare them with the baseline, a probe on the top 19 source PCs by variance, and a probe on the 81 PCs left after ablating the interp-selected set (Figure 5).

The interp-selected probe beats the baseline and the variance control on all 3 targets, by wide margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. It also beats the ablated-81 probe on all 3 targets. Gap closed is defined as (interp − baseline) / (greedy − baseline). On Insider Trading Report, interp selection closes 78% of the gap between the baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929). On Sandbagging, it closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832). On Insider Trading Confirm, the baseline is near ceiling, and every method except the ablated set performs similarly, so this target is uninformative.

## 5 Limitations

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Insider Trading Confirm is uninformative because baseline transfer already reaches 0.874. Generalization to other model families and datasets is untested.

Sandbagging margins are small.
On Sandbagging, interp selection raises AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, which recovers 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound (0.832). Sandbagging is also the most out-of-distribution target. The Insider Trading Report result is more robust: 0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929.

Linear pipeline.
The pipeline is fully linear (PCA projection followed by logistic regression), so the existence of a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising. We have not tested nonlinear probes or other readout locations.

No causal validation.
Our claims about what each PC "encodes" rest on top-activating examples and the judge's verbalizations. They are descriptive, not causal. We have not ablated high-scoring PCs at inference time.

## 6 Conclusion

In probe-based deception monitoring, a small subset of source-domain PCs supports cross-domain transfer that nearly matches target-trained probes. This subset is not recovered by source-side or target-side separability. An LLM-judge interpretability score over each PC's top-activating examples, computed without target data, partially recovers it. These results suggest treating OOD probing as a representation-selection problem: alongside fitting a classifier, one must choose a subspace that keeps the intended behavioral feature and excludes dataset-specific cues.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes can be used to detect behaviors and concepts inside language model activations, but may fail to transfer to out-of-distribution examples. We study the generalization of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on a single source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets, and we propose to analyze this problem in the basis of principal components (PCs) of the source-domain activations rather than in the raw activation space. Within this basis, we lay out a set of complementary subspace-selection procedures: a target-guided greedy search that serves as a reference point, rankings derived from the standardized weights of source-trained and target-trained probes, and an interpretability-driven procedure in which an LLM judge scores natural-language descriptions of each PC's most and least activating examples for their likely relevance to out-of-distribution deception. We describe each procedure, the controls we pair it with, and the practical considerations involved in applying it, including how to standardize target data, how to handle ambiguous labels, and how to reduce noise in judge scores. Broadly, we argue that the out-of-distribution robustness of probes is usefully studied as a question of subspace selection, and that interpretable bases such as source PCs make this question tractable to investigate.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are standard tooling for reading information from language model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019).
Linear probes are cheap to train and expose some semantically meaningful information in the otherwise uninterpretable representation space.
However, probes that look strong in-distribution are sometimes unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026). Existing work shows that key behavioral concepts are linearly represented in model activations (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), so probes should have the capacity to detect these concepts, yet they appear to learn spurious correlations in practice (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). This is unacceptable for probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions, setting a clear challenge:
how can we build probes that only learn generalizing features?

To tackle this, we work in the basis of source-domain principal components (PCs) rather than raw activations, avoiding the assumption that the model's latent dimensions provide a privileged basis. Principal components offer a simple, data-driven way to study structure in representation spaces, and prior work even suggests that the choice of PCs matters: Mu et al. (2018) shows that removing the top PCs of an embedding space improves downstream performance, and Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. Thus, the focus of our investigation becomes: which subset of principal components supports generalizable probe training and how can that subset be identified?

The PC basis has several attractive properties for this question. First, it is computed entirely from source data, so any selection procedure defined over it can in principle be applied before a deployment distribution is known. Second, each PC is a single direction with a well-defined positive and negative pole, so its behavior can be inspected by looking at the examples that activate it most strongly in either direction. Third, a subset of PCs defines an orthogonal subspace, which makes it straightforward to train, compare, and ablate probes restricted to different subsets while keeping all other parts of the pipeline fixed.

We use deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) as our testbed,
training them on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluating on 3 held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging) (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).
Working in the source-domain PCA basis, we explore strategies for selecting a subset of training dimensions that avoid spurious correlations and transfer to target domains.

Deception is a natural testbed for this kind of study. The behavior of interest, a model knowingly asserting something it believes to be false, is conceptually stable across settings, but the surface form in which it appears varies enormously: a roleplayed excuse, a misleading trading report, and a deliberately incorrect answer on a capability evaluation share little vocabulary or structure. A probe that latches onto the vocabulary of one setting will therefore fail on the others, while a probe that captures the underlying contrast should not. This makes the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution behavior especially visible.

This work contributes the following:

•

A subspace-selection framing of probe transfer (Section 4.2).
We formulate cross-domain probe transfer in terms of which source PCs a probe is permitted to use, and define a target-guided greedy search over source PCs as a reference procedure for this question.

•

Weight-based selection rules
(Section 4.3). We describe how to rank PCs by the standardized weights of source-trained or target-trained probes, giving two simple hypotheses about which directions might be relevant for transfer.

•

An interpretability-driven selection rule that uses no target data (Section 4.5).
We describe a procedure in which an LLM judge interprets each PC and rates how likely it is to encode a transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns, and we use these ratings to define a candidate probe subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

A related line of work studies whether high-level behavioral or semantic properties are represented as directions or low-dimensional subspaces in activation space. Marks and Tegmark (2024) report linear structure in true/false representations across datasets, while Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and connect it to both probing and steering. Similarly, Zou et al. (2025) model high-level properties such as honesty and emotion as population-level directions that can be read from and intervened on in model activations.

This perspective has also been used to explain and control model behavior. (Arditi et al., 2024) show that a single direction can mediate refusal behavior, suggesting that some high-level behaviors may be localized in simple linear features. Lu et al. (2026) similarly identify an "assistant" axis corresponding to assistant-like behavior. Together, these works suggest that linear structure can support both mechanistic understanding and activation-space interventions, while also raising questions about when such directions capture stable concepts rather than context-dependent correlations.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Linear and lightweight probes have a long history in interpretability as tools for analyzing what information is represented in neural networks (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Recent work has applied such probes to safety-relevant signals in LLM activations, including latent truthfulness without direct supervision (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

At the same time, methodological skepticism is central to the probing literature. Hewitt and Liang (2019) argue that high probe accuracy alone is insufficient evidence that a model already represents the target property, since the probe may itself learn the task or exploit surface-level correlates. Similarly, Ravichander et al. (2021) question whether probing reliably establishes what information is encoded or merely recoverable. Recent work also finds that probes with strong in-distribution performance can generalize unevenly out of distribution (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini). These concerns motivate careful evaluation of whether safety probes identify robust internal signals rather than dataset-specific artifacts.

A recurring theme across this literature is that the quality of a probe cannot be judged from in-distribution accuracy alone. Control tasks, selectivity measures, and held-out evaluation sets have all been proposed as ways of separating what a representation encodes from what a sufficiently flexible classifier can extract. Our setting adds a further dimension to this concern: even when the probe is a simple linear model, the particular direction it learns may combine signal that is genuinely about the behavior with signal that merely co-occurs with the behavior in the training data.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

Another approach aims to interpret internal representations by assigning natural-language descriptions to neurons or learned features. Bills et al. (2023) introduced the use of LLMs to generate explanations of neurons from high-activation examples. This approach has since been extended to the automatic labeling of features in sparse autoencoders ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)), enabling large-scale interpretation of learned feature dictionaries.

Recent work has further explored whether natural-language feature descriptions can be used not only for interpretation but also for intervention. For example, Casademunt et al. (2025) identify concepts through automated natural-language interpretation and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior. Our interpretability-driven procedure follows this line of work, applying automated explanation to PCs rather than to neurons or dictionary features, and using the resulting descriptions to decide which directions a probe should be allowed to use.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

Following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025), we use 4 of their deception detection datasets (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging), with descriptions being provided in Appendix A.

Roleplaying is our source domain and the other 3 are target test sets. Each response is labeled as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) by GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024), with the ambiguous responses being removed for our experiments.

The three targets span a range of distances from the source. Insider Trading Report and Insider Trading Confirm share a scenario with each other but not with Roleplaying, and differ in whether the deceptive act is an initial omission or a later explicit confirmation. Sandbagging differs from the source both in topic and in the form deception takes, since the dishonesty consists of deliberately wrong answers rather than misleading statements about events.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the layer with the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. To extract activations, we pass each prompt through the model and average token activations over just the assistant's response.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

We standardize source activations to zero mean and unit variance, then apply the same source statistics to standardize all target activations. We run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. All probes are logistic regression classifiers ( $\lambda=10$ ); for experiments using a subset $S$ of these 100 PCs, activations are projected onto $S$ before training and evaluation, while the baseline probes train directly on the full standardized activations.

Using source statistics for standardizing the targets is deliberate. Re-standardizing each target with its own statistics would leak distributional information about the target into the representation and blur the distinction between source-only and target-informed procedures. Fixing the transformation on the source keeps every selection rule comparable in what it is allowed to see.

We use the top 100 PCs because alignment with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index (Appendix C), meaning lower-index PCs are more amenable to natural-language interpretation and hence comparable with interpretability-driven selection methods. This is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better; it is a choice made so that every direction considered by the selection procedures below is one that can plausibly be described in natural language.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe configurations used as reference points: source-trained probes on full representations, source-trained probes on the top-100 PCs, and target-trained probes on the top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV).

Our reference point is a probe trained on the full standardized source representations and evaluated directly on each target. This is the configuration most commonly used in practice, and any subspace-selection rule should be judged by whether it improves on it.

We pair this baseline with two further configurations. The first is a source-trained probe restricted to the top-100 source PCs, which isolates the effect of the dimensionality reduction itself from the effect of later selection steps. The second is a probe trained on target data within the same 100-PC subspace using 5-fold cross-validation. This configuration is not a deployable method, since it requires labeled target examples, but it is useful for interpretation: it indicates how much target-relevant signal the subspace contains when the probe is free to place its weight wherever the target data suggests.

Taken together, these three configurations define the space within which source-only selection rules operate. A selection rule can only reweight or discard directions that already exist in the 100-PC basis, so comparisons between source-trained and target-trained probes within that basis are the natural frame for the procedures that follow.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Configurations compared in the subspace-existence analysis: the full-representation baseline, top-k PCs by variance (k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs.

The central question of this section is whether a subset of source PCs can be found on which a source-trained probe transfers well, and how such a subset might be characterized.
To study this, we introduce a greedy algorithm for PC selection.
Starting from an empty set, we iteratively add PCs from the source dataset.
At each step, we search over the top 100 PCs and add the one that most improves AUROC on the target.
To evaluate each candidate, we project source activations onto the current subset and train a logistic regression probe on those projections.

Probe weights are always fit on source data, but the choice of PC subsets is guided by performance on labeled examples from the target dataset.
Using 5-fold cross-validation over the target dataset, we perform greedy PC selection on the non-held-out target folds and evaluate the selected source-trained probe on the held-out target fold. We stop when no candidate PC improves AUROC by more than 0.001.

The greedy probe should be read as an upper bound on transfer performance, not an unbiased OOD estimate, because subset selection uses some target examples. Its role is diagnostic: it asks how well a source-trained probe could do if the right directions were chosen, independently of whether those directions could be identified without target data.
To ground this reference point, we compare against simply selecting the top $k$ PCs by variance, where $k$ matches the number of PCs selected by the greedy algorithm. This control tests whether any advantage of a selected subset is attributable merely to its size or to the amount of source variance it captures, rather than to the identity of the chosen directions.

Greedy forward selection has well-known weaknesses. It can miss subsets whose members are individually unhelpful but jointly useful, and its output depends on the stopping threshold. We accept these limitations because the procedure is simple, its behavior is easy to inspect, and the subsets it returns are small enough to be examined direction by direction in later sections.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: PC-selection rules compared in this section: ranking by source-probe weights, by target-probe weights, and greedy oracle selection.

What property might make a PC transferable, and can that property be detected from the source side alone?
To approach this, we consider 2 simple hypotheses about what a transferable subset would contain.
The first posits that the transferable PCs are simply the ones that separate the target classes well by themselves across the test set, so that a target-guided procedure would pick them because it has access to target data.
The second posits that they are the PCs the source probe already leans on most heavily, so that a target-guided procedure would merely be rediscovering the source signal in a more compact form.

We compare 2 rankings of PCs, both based on the standardized coefficient (the absolute value of each probe coefficient multiplied by the standard deviation of the corresponding PC) given to each PC by a probe trained on activations projected on the source-PCA basis.

The 'source-PCA probe' ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on source data, while the 'target-PCA probe' ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on target data. In both cases, the activations are projected onto the source-PCA basis.
In both cases, the probes are then trained on source data that has been projected onto the top $k$ PCs, selected according to their respective rankings.
Each hypothesis makes a concrete prediction: if it were correct, the corresponding ranking should behave like the greedy reference.

To set $k$ , we run the greedy method on the full target dataset rather than per fold, giving a single stable PC set whose size determines $k$ for each target. Because this uses the full dataset rather than cross-validation, the resulting subset is not identical to the per-fold subsets described in the previous section.

The two hypotheses are worth distinguishing because they suggest different remedies. If transferable directions were simply the most target-discriminative ones, improving transfer would be a matter of acquiring a small amount of target data. If they were the most source-discriminative ones, the problem would lie in regularization or in the compactness of the representation. Neither remedy addresses the possibility that transfer depends on a property of directions that is not captured by discriminability on either domain, which motivates the interpretability analysis that follows.
Further details on the PC sets involved are given in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

A complementary way to characterize candidate directions is to ask what each one encodes in human-interpretable terms.
To do this, we adopt the interpretability method of Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025).

For each of the top 100 source PCs, we find the 8 most and 8 least PC-activating examples from the source data, before prompting an LLM to generate a natural-language description of the positive pole, the negative pole, and the PC direction as a whole.
The LLM judge then rates the generalizability of each direction on a 1–10 scale (OOD score), with the full judge prompt and model detail being provided in Appendix B.

The judge prompt is designed to push against two failure modes. The first is overgeneralization, in which a direction with a narrow and specific pattern is described in broad terms such as sentiment or honesty. The second is overrating surface cues, in which a direction that tracks lexical habits or task-specific phrasing is scored as generally useful because it happens to correlate with deception in the source examples. The prompt therefore asks for the narrowest accurate description and reserves high scores for directions that seem tied to a general strategy rather than to local wording.

Because the judge sees only source examples, its scores are available before any target data is collected. This is the property that distinguishes the interpretability procedure from the selection rules of the previous two sections, and it is what makes it a candidate for a deployable selection method rather than a diagnostic one.
Examples of the judge's output format are discussed in Appendix E.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Configurations compared for interpretability-based selection: the interp-selected subspace versus three controls, namely the full-representation baseline, the top PCs by variance with matched size, and the remaining PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs.

Building on the OOD scores, we define a probe subspace consisting of the PCs that received the highest observed score from the judge, and train a source probe on activations projected onto this subspace. No target data is used at any point in this procedure.
Because LLM judge scores are noisy, we run the scoring twice and only keep PCs that received the highest score in both runs. Requiring agreement across runs trades recall for precision: some useful directions may be discarded, but the retained set is less likely to include directions that were scored highly by chance.

We evaluate the interp-selected probe against three controls. The first is the full-representation baseline from Section 4.1. The second is a probe trained on the same number of top source PCs by variance, which tests whether the selected subspace behaves differently from an arbitrary low-dimensional projection of the same size. The third is a probe trained on the complement of the selected PCs within the top 100, which tests whether the directions removed by the selection are themselves the ones that carry transferable signal.

These controls are designed to rule out the most obvious alternative explanations for any difference between the interp-selected probe and the baseline. Dimensionality reduction alone, a preference for high-variance directions, and the mere removal of directions are each addressed by one control. The greedy reference from Section 4.2 provides an additional point of comparison, indicating how much room for improvement exists on each target for any source-trained probe within the 100-PC basis.

We expect the informativeness of these comparisons to vary across targets. Where the baseline already transfers well, there is little headroom for any selection rule to distinguish itself. Where the target is far from the source, as with Sandbagging, the comparisons are more demanding and more revealing of whether a selection rule has captured something general.

## 5 Limitations

Our framework is narrow in scope and there are several limitations that should be considered by the reader.

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and a single source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Moreover, one target, Insider Trading Confirm, is relatively easy for the baseline, which limits how much it can discriminate between selection rules. Whether the framework behaves similarly for other model families or other datasets is an open question we leave to future work.

Distribution shift varies by target.
Sandbagging is the most out-of-distribution target, and any selection rule restricted to source PCs is limited by how well the source basis covers the directions relevant to that target. Conclusions drawn from a single distant target should be treated with caution, and a broader collection of targets at varying distances from the source would make the framework more informative.

Linear pipeline. Our probe pipeline is fully linear (PCA projection followed by logistic regression), so the subspaces it studies are linear by construction. Whether the same framing extends to nonlinear probes or other readout locations remains an open question.

Judge reliability.
The OOD score depends on a single judge model and a single prompt. Different judges, prompts, or numbers of exemplars could produce different rankings, and our two-run agreement filter mitigates only some of this variability.

No causal validation.
Any structural claims about what a PC "encodes" are based on top-activating examples and an LLM judge's verbalization of the contrast.
These are descriptive claims, not causal ones. We have not ablated PCs during inference to verify that they carry the contrast they appear to encode.

## 6 Conclusion

We have presented a framework for studying out-of-distribution deception probing in terms of subspace selection over source-domain principal components. Within this framework we defined a target-guided greedy reference procedure, two weight-based ranking rules corresponding to simple hypotheses about transferable directions, and an interpretability-driven rule in which an LLM judge scores natural-language descriptions of each PC without access to target data, together with controls that isolate the effects of dimensionality, variance, and ablation.

A key motivation is that robust probing requires identifying not only whether a behavioral signal is linearly accessible, but where in activation space that signal is represented. Linear probes trained over full representations may combine general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues. These heuristics can support high in-distribution accuracy while hurting transfer. Sparse subspaces of interpretable directions offer a way to make this distinction explicit. This frames OOD probing as a representation-selection problem: the goal is not only to fit a classifier, but also to choose a subspace that preserves the intended behavioral feature and filters out spurious correlation. We hope that the procedures described here provide a useful starting point for future work along these lines.

## Appendix D PC Set Comparisons

The selection rules in Section 4.3 each produce a ranked list of PCs, and comparing these lists is a natural way to understand how the rules relate to one another. A convenient summary is the Jaccard overlap between the PC sets returned by two methods for the same target, which measures the fraction of selected directions they share. Low overlap indicates that two rules are drawing on largely different parts of the representation space, while high overlap indicates that they agree on which directions matter.
