Most of these directions lie among the lowest-index PCs, which is unsurprising since low-index PCs capture the largest share of source variance and the source probe is trained on the same distribution. Whether such directions reflect the behavioral contrast itself or features specific to the Roleplaying scenarios is exactly the question the interpretability procedure is designed to address.

## Appendix E PC Interpretability

For each PC, the judge returns a description of the positive pole, a description of the negative pole, a summary of the shared direction, and an OOD usefulness score with a short justification. In practice, the justifications tend to fall into a small number of recurring patterns. Many directions are described as contrasts between denial or deflection on one side and admission or detailed explanation on the other. The judge frequently qualifies such descriptions by noting reliance on explicit lexical markers such as "Yes" and "No", on hedging phrases, or on domain-specific vocabulary, and lowers its score accordingly.

Other directions are described primarily in stylistic terms, such as assertiveness, formality, or the use of enumerations and résumé-like phrasing. These are typically judged to be surface cues that could correlate with deception in a particular dataset without reflecting a general strategy. A smaller number of directions are described in terms of communicative tactics, such as defensive or public-relations-style hedging, which the judge treats as more plausibly general while still flagging the risk of false positives from legitimate uses of the same tactics.

The judge's justifications also make explicit the trade-off between generality and reliability that motivates the prompt design. Directions tied to broad tactics are rated as more likely to transfer but are frequently characterized as noisy, while directions tied to narrow lexical patterns are rated as brittle even when they appear clean within the source data. This pattern is consistent with the instructions in Appendix B, and it illustrates the kind of distinction the interpretability-driven selection rule relies on when assembling a candidate subspace.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes are used to detect behaviors and concepts in language model activations, but their out-of-distribution transfer is unreliable. We study Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on a single source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Source-trained logistic probes restricted to a small, target-selected subset of source-domain principal components (PCs) approach the AUROC of probes trained directly on the target distribution. Restricting instead to PCs whose 8 most/least activating source examples receive the maximum generalizability score from an LLM judge, with no target data, closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Rankings by source-probe or target-probe standardized weights do not recover the oracle subsets. Judge descriptions of oracle-selected PCs contrast response strategies, whereas those of the most heavily source-weighted PCs reference explicit lexical markers. We frame OOD probe robustness in terms of subspace selection.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are standard tooling for reading information from language model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019); they are cheap to train and expose semantically meaningful structure in an otherwise opaque representation space. Probes with strong in-distribution performance are, however, often unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026). Key behavioral concepts are linearly represented in activations (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), yet probes trained on them pick up spurious correlations in practice (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), which undermines probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions.

We work in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, so as not to treat the model's latent dimensions as a privileged basis. PC choice is known to matter downstream: Mu et al. (2018) improve embedding performance by removing top PCs, and Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. We ask which subsets of source PCs support transferable probe training and whether they can be identified without target labels.

The testbed is deception probing on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), trained on Roleplaying deception scenarios and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Contributions:

•

A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2). A target-supervised greedy search over source PCs returns 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.

•

Source-side and target-side rankings both fail to recover the subspace (Section 4.3). Selecting PCs by the standardized weights of a source-trained or target-trained probe does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline in general.

•

An LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data (Section 4.5). Selecting PCs by a judge's OOD score computed from source examples alone improves transfer on the two hard targets.

Figure 1: Overview of PC-based subspace selection for OOD deception probing. Activations are projected onto the source-domain PCA basis, candidate PC directions are filtered, and probes are trained on the selected low-dimensional subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

Several works study whether high-level behavioral or semantic properties correspond to directions or low-dimensional subspaces of activation space. Marks and Tegmark (2024) report linear structure in true/false representations across datasets; Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and relate it to probing and steering; Zou et al. (2025) treat properties such as honesty and emotion as population-level directions that can be read and intervened on.

The same perspective has been used to explain and control behavior. Arditi et al. (2024) find a single direction mediating refusal, and Lu et al. (2026) identify an "assistant" axis for assistant-like behavior. These results support both mechanistic analysis and activation-space intervention, while leaving open when such directions capture stable concepts as opposed to context-dependent correlates.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Linear and lightweight probes have long been used to analyze what information networks represent (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Recent applications to LLM safety signals include latent truthfulness without direct supervision (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

Hewitt and Liang (2019) argue that probe accuracy alone does not establish that a model represents a property, since the probe may learn the task or exploit surface correlates; Ravichander et al. (2021) question whether probing shows what is encoded rather than merely recoverable. Probes with strong in-distribution performance also generalize unevenly out of distribution (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini), raising the question of whether safety probes track robust internal signals or dataset-specific artifacts.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

A separate line of work assigns natural-language descriptions to neurons or learned features. Bills et al. (2023) used LLMs to explain neurons from high-activation examples, and the approach has been extended to automatic labeling of sparse autoencoder features ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)), enabling large-scale interpretation of feature dictionaries.

Such descriptions have also been used for intervention: Casademunt et al. (2025) identify concepts by automated natural-language interpretation and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

Following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025), we use 4 of their deception detection datasets (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging), described in Appendix A.

Roleplaying is the source domain; the other 3 are target test sets. GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) labels each response honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous responses are removed throughout.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the layer with the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. Each prompt is passed through the model and token activations are mean-pooled over the assistant response only.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same source statistics are applied to all target activations. PCA is fit on the scaled source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic regression ( $\lambda=10$ ); for a subset $S$ of the 100 PCs, activations are projected onto $S$ before training and evaluation, while baseline probes are trained on the full standardized activations.

The cutoff of 100 is motivated by alignment with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023), which decreases with PC index (Appendix C); low-index PCs are thus more amenable to natural-language interpretation and comparable across interpretability-driven selection methods. No claim is made that low-index PCs generalize better; the sufficiency of the 100-PC subspace is checked in Section 4.1.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Error bars: 95% CIs

Source-trained probes on full representations reach 0.874 AUROC on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging (Figure 2). Source-trained probes on the top-100 PCs are also reported.

Probes trained directly on target data within the 100-PC subspace, under 5-fold cross-validation, reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC on the three targets, so deceptive and honest responses are separable on every target within this subspace. The shortfall of source-trained probes is therefore attributable to the direction they fit within it.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the full-representation baseline (blue), top-k PCs by variance (teal, k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Greedy oracle selection starts from the empty set and, at each step, searches the top 100 PCs and adds the one whose inclusion most improves target AUROC, where each candidate subset is scored by projecting source activations onto it, fitting a logistic regression probe on the projections, and evaluating on target data. Probe weights are always fit on source data; only subset membership is target-guided. Selection is run under 5-fold cross-validation over the target dataset: greedy search uses the non-held-out folds, and the resulting source-trained probe is evaluated on the held-out fold. Search terminates when no candidate improves AUROC by more than 0.001. Selected subsets average 15 PCs for Insider Trading Report, 8 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging.

Because selection consumes target labels, the greedy probe is an upper bound on transfer, not an unbiased OOD estimate. The control selects the top $k$ PCs by explained variance, with $k$ matched to the greedy subset size (Figure 3).

Greedy approaches target-trained performance on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, improving on the baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC respectively. The variance control matches greedy only on Insider Trading Confirm and falls far behind on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Probe AUROC across the three targets for three PC-selection rules: ranking by source-probe weights (red), by target-probe weights (pink), and greedy oracle selection (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We test 2 hypotheses about the greedy subsets: (i) they consist of PCs that individually separate the target classes well, which greedy finds by virtue of target access; (ii) they consist of the PCs the source probe already weights most heavily, recovered in compressed form.

Both rankings use the standardized coefficient, i.e. the absolute value of each probe coefficient multiplied by the standard deviation of the corresponding PC, from a probe on activations projected onto the source-PCA basis. The 'source-PCA probe' ranking uses a probe trained on source data; the 'target-PCA probe' ranking uses a probe trained on target data. In both cases a fresh probe is then trained on source data projected onto the top $k$ PCs under the respective ranking. Under (i) the target-PCA ranking, and under (ii) the source-PCA ranking, should match greedy.

$k$ is set by running greedy on the full target dataset rather than per fold, which yields a single PC set: $k=13$ for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. Greedy numbers in this section therefore differ slightly from the cross-validated numbers of Section 4.2 (Figure 4).

The source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. The target-PCA probe performs well on Insider Trading Report, worse than greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, and below chance on Sandbagging. Neither hypothesis holds. Overlaps between selected sets are given in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Following Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025), for each of the top 100 source PCs we collect the 8 most and 8 least PC-activating source examples and prompt an LLM to describe the positive pole, the negative pole, and the shared direction, and to rate the direction's usefulness for out-of-distribution deception detection on a 1–10 scale (OOD score); the prompt and model are given in Appendix B. No PC scored above 6, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed score, and PCs attaining it in both of two runs are retained, yielding 19 PCs.

Five PCs occur in the greedy selections of more than one target; 3 of these 5 received the maximum OOD score. Of the top 5 PCs by source-PCA probe weight, 1 received the maximum score. Descriptions of the shared greedy PCs (e.g. deny/deflect vs provide details for PC62, hedging and defensive PR-style wording for PC86) are framed as response strategies, while the heavily source-weighted PC7 and PC8 are described in terms of explicit "No"/"Yes" turns and common denial phrasing. Per-PC judge outputs are in Appendix E.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the interp-selected subspace (red; 19 PCs) versus three controls: full-representation baseline (blue), top-19 PCs by variance (teal), and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs (brown). Error bars: 95% CIs.

The interp-selected subspace consists of the PCs receiving the maximum OOD score in both judge runs (the two-run intersection mitigates judge noise), 19 PCs in total; no target data enter selection. Controls are a probe on the ablated complement (the 81 PCs not selected) and a probe on the top 19 source PCs by variance (Figure 5).

The interp-selected probe outperforms the baseline on all 3 targets, outperforms the variance control by wide margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, and outperforms the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. Defining gap closed as (interp − baseline)/(greedy − baseline), interp selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and greedy (0.929) on Insider Trading Report, and 25% of the gap between baseline and greedy (0.832) on Sandbagging. On Insider Trading Confirm the baseline is near ceiling and all selection methods other than interp-ablated perform comparably, so this target is uninformative.

## 5 Limitations

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and one source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Insider Trading Confirm is uninformative because baseline transfer already reaches 0.874. Generalization to other model families and datasets is untested.

Sandbagging margins are small.
On Sandbagging, interp selection raises AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, recovering 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound (0.832). Sandbagging is also the most out-of-distribution target, which plausibly limits the gain. The Insider Trading Report result (0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929) is the more robust.

Linear pipeline. The pipeline is fully linear (PCA projection followed by logistic regression), so the existence of a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising. Extension to nonlinear probes or other readout locations is open.

No causal validation.
Claims about what each PC "encodes" rest on top-activating examples and the judge's verbalization of the contrast, and are descriptive rather than causal. High-scoring PCs have not been ablated at inference to verify that they carry the apparent contrast.

## 6 Conclusion

In probe-based deception monitoring, a small subset of source-domain PCs supports cross-domain transfer that nearly matches target-trained probes, and this subset is not recovered by source-side or target-side weight rankings. An LLM-judge interpretability score over each PC's top- and bottom-activating source examples, with no target access, partially recovers it.

Robust probing thus depends not only on whether a behavioral signal is linearly accessible but on where in activation space it is read out. Full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues that support in-distribution accuracy while hurting transfer, whereas sparse PC subspaces can isolate more general behavioral structure. OOD probing then becomes a representation-selection problem: choosing a subspace that preserves the intended behavioral feature and excludes spurious correlates, in addition to fitting a classifier.

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

Linear probes can be used to detect behaviors and concepts inside language model activations, but may fail to transfer to out-of-distribution examples. We study the generalization of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on a single source dataset and evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets, working in the basis of the top 100 source-domain principal components (PCs). Source-trained probes restricted to a target-selected subset of 8–15 PCs nearly match probes trained directly on the test distribution, whereas subsets chosen by explained variance, by source-probe weight, or by target-probe weight do not. Scoring each PC with an LLM judge on whether its most and least activating source examples imply a transferable deception direction, and probing only on the highest-scoring PCs, closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging, with no target data used for selection.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes are standard tooling for reading information from language model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019).
They are cheap to train and recover semantically meaningful information from the residual stream.
Probes that look strong in-distribution are, however, sometimes unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026). Key behavioral concepts are linearly represented in model activations (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), yet probes trained on them appear to pick up spurious correlations in practice (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), a concern for probe-based monitoring of harmful interactions.

We work in the basis of source-domain principal components rather than raw activations, so as not to treat the model’s latent dimensions as a privileged basis. Prior work indicates that the choice of PCs affects downstream behavior: Mu et al. (2018) show that removing the top PCs of an embedding space improves downstream performance, and Kantamneni et al. (2025) use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. We ask which subset of principal components supports generalizable probe training and how that subset can be identified.

The testbed is deception probing on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), with probes trained on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging) (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Within the source-domain PCA basis, we compare strategies for selecting the training dimensions of a source-trained probe.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

A related line of work studies whether high-level behavioral or semantic properties are represented as directions or low-dimensional subspaces in activation space. Marks and Tegmark (2024) report linear structure in true/false representations across datasets, while Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and connect it to both probing and steering. Zou et al. (2025) model high-level properties such as honesty and emotion as population-level directions that can be read from and intervened on in model activations.

This perspective has also been used to explain and control model behavior. Arditi et al. (2024) show that a single direction can mediate refusal behavior, suggesting that some high-level behaviors may be localized in simple linear features. Lu et al. (2026) identify an “assistant” axis corresponding to assistant-like behavior. These works support both mechanistic understanding and activation-space interventions, while leaving open when such directions capture stable concepts rather than context-dependent correlations.

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Linear and lightweight probes have a long history in interpretability as tools for analyzing what information is represented in neural networks (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Recent work has applied such probes to safety-relevant signals in LLM activations, including latent truthfulness without direct supervision (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

Methodological skepticism is central to the probing literature. Hewitt and Liang (2019) argue that high probe accuracy alone is insufficient evidence that a model already represents the target property, since the probe may itself learn the task or exploit surface-level correlates. Ravichander et al. (2021) question whether probing reliably establishes what information is encoded or merely recoverable. Probes with strong in-distribution performance can also generalize unevenly out of distribution (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini), motivating evaluation of whether safety probes identify robust internal signals rather than dataset-specific artifacts.

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

Another approach interprets internal representations by assigning natural-language descriptions to neurons or learned features. Bills et al. (2023) introduced the use of LLMs to generate explanations of neurons from high-activation examples. This has been extended to the automatic labeling of features in sparse autoencoders ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)), enabling large-scale interpretation of learned feature dictionaries.

Natural-language feature descriptions have also been used for intervention: Casademunt et al. (2025) identify concepts through automated natural-language interpretation and ablate them during fine-tuning to reduce misaligned behavior.

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

Following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025), we use 4 of their deception detection datasets (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging), described in Appendix A.

Roleplaying is the source domain and the other 3 are target test sets. Each response is labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1) by GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024); ambiguous responses are removed throughout.

#### Language models.

Following Ying et al. (2026), we use layer 15 residual stream activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the layer with the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. Each prompt is passed through the model and token activations are averaged over the assistant’s response only.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Source activations are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and the same source statistics are applied to all target activations. PCA is run on the scaled source activations and the top 100 PCs are retained. All probes are logistic regression classifiers ( $\lambda=10$ ) evaluated by AUROC; for a subset $S$ of the 100 PCs, activations are projected onto $S$ before training and evaluation, while baseline probes train directly on the full standardized activations.

The top 100 PCs are used because alignment with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index (Appendix C), so lower-index PCs are better suited to natural-language interpretation and comparable with interpretability-driven selection. No claim is made that low-index PCs generalize better; Section 4.1 checks the information content of the 100-PC subspace on every target.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Error bars: 95% CIs

Probes trained on the full source representations and evaluated on each target (Figure 2) reach 0.874 AUROC on Insider Trading Confirm, 0.706 on Insider Trading Report, and 0.606 on Sandbagging.

A probe trained directly on target data within the 100-PC source subspace, using 5-fold cross-validation, reaches 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the full-representation baseline (blue), top-k PCs by variance (teal, k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We next consider greedy PC selection. Starting from an empty set, PCs are added one at a time: at each step every remaining candidate among the top 100 PCs is evaluated by projecting source activations onto the current subset plus the candidate, fitting a logistic regression probe on those source projections, and measuring AUROC on the target; the candidate yielding the largest improvement is added.

Probe weights are always fit on source data, while subset choice is guided by labeled target examples. Under 5-fold cross-validation over the target dataset, greedy selection is run on the non-held-out target folds and the resulting source-trained probe is evaluated on the held-out fold. The search terminates when no candidate improves AUROC by more than 0.001, converging on 15 PCs on average for Insider Trading Report, 8 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging.

Since subset selection consumes target examples, the greedy probe is an upper bound on transfer performance rather than an unbiased OOD estimate. As a control we select the top $k$ PCs by variance, with $k$ matched to the greedy subset size (Figure 3).

The greedy probe approaches the target-trained probe on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, improving on the baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 points of AUROC, respectively. The variance control matches greedy only on Insider Trading Confirm and falls well behind on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Probe AUROC across the three targets for three PC-selection rules: ranking by source-probe weights (red), by target-probe weights (pink), and greedy oracle selection (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

We test 2 hypotheses about the greedy subset. Under the first, the transferable PCs are those that individually separate the target classes well across the test set, which greedy recovers through its access to target data. Under the second, they are the PCs the source probe already weights most heavily, so that greedy merely compresses the source signal.

Both are tested via the standardized coefficient given to each PC by a probe on activations projected onto the source-PCA basis. The ‘source-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights of such a probe fit on source data; the ‘target-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights of such a probe fit on target data. In either case, a probe is then trained on source data projected onto the top $k$ PCs under the respective ranking, and either hypothesis predicts recovery of greedy performance.

$k$ is set by running greedy on the full target dataset rather than per fold, giving a single stable PC set: $k=13$ for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 14 for Sandbagging. The greedy figures here therefore differ slightly from the cross-validated figures of Section 4.2 (Figure 4).

The source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. The target-PCA probe does well on Insider Trading Report, is worse than greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, and falls below chance on Sandbagging. Set overlaps are given in Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Following Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025), for each of the top 100 source PCs we retrieve the 8 most and 8 least PC-activating source examples and prompt an LLM to describe the positive pole, the negative pole, and the shared direction. The judge then rates the usefulness of the direction for out-of-distribution deception detection on a 1–10 scale (OOD score); the prompt and model are given in Appendix B.
No PC received an OOD score above 6 on the judge’s 1–10 scale, so 6 is treated as the maximum observed OOD score, and PCs reaching it in both of two scoring runs are retained, yielding 19 PCs.

5 PCs appear in the greedy selections of more than one target; 3 of these 5 received the maximum OOD score. Of the top 5 PCs selected by the source-PCA probes, only 1 received the maximum OOD score. Per-PC interpretations for both groups are listed in Appendix E.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the interp-selected subspace (red; 19 PCs) versus three controls: full-representation baseline (blue), top-19 PCs by variance (teal), and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs (brown). Error bars: 95% CIs.

The 19 PCs scoring the maximum OOD score in both runs form the interp-selected subspace; the two-run requirement accounts for noise in the judge scores. No target data enter this selection. Controls are a probe on the ablated complement (the 81 PCs not selected) and a probe on the top 19 source PCs by variance (Figure 5).

The interp-selected probe outperforms the baseline and the variance control on all 3 targets, by wide margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, and outperforms the interp-ablated probe on all 3 targets. We report gap closed as (interp AUROC − baseline) / (greedy AUROC − baseline).
On Insider Trading Report, interp-selection closes 78% of the gap between baseline (0.706) and the greedy oracle (0.929).
On Insider Trading Confirm, baseline transfer is already near ceiling and all methods other than the interp-ablated probe perform comparably.
On Sandbagging, interp-selection closes 25% of the gap to the greedy oracle (0.832).

## 5 Limitations

Our strongest claims are narrow, and several limitations apply.

Single model and source dataset.
All experiments use a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15) and a single source dataset (Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)). Insider Trading Confirm results are uninformative, as baseline transfer there already reaches 0.874. Generalization to other model families or datasets is left to future work.

Sandbagging margins are small.
On Sandbagging, interpretability selection raises AUROC from 0.606 to 0.662, recovering only 25% of the gap to the greedy upper bound (0.832). Sandbagging is also the most out-of-distribution target, and the modest gain likely reflects this distribution shift.
The Insider Trading Report result (0.706 to 0.881, closing 78% of the gap to greedy at 0.929) is the more robust.

Linear pipeline. The probe pipeline is fully linear (PCA projection followed by logistic regression), so the existence of a transferable subspace is perhaps unsurprising. Extension to nonlinear probes or other readout locations remains open.

No causal validation.
Claims about what each PC “encodes” rest on top-activating examples and an LLM judge’s verbalization of the contrast; they are descriptive, not causal. High-scoring PCs have not been ablated during inference to verify that they carry the contrast attributed to them.

## 6 Conclusion

In probe-based deception monitoring, a small subset of source-domain principal components (PCs) supports cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes, and this subset is not recovered by source-side or target-side separability rankings.
An LLM judge’s interpretability score over each PC’s top-activating examples, computed without target data, partially recovers it.

Robust probing thus depends not only on whether a behavioral signal is linearly accessible but on where in activation space the probe reads it. Full-representation probes may mix general behavioral features with dataset-specific cues that raise in-distribution accuracy while hurting transfer, whereas sparse PC subspaces may isolate more general behavioral structure. OOD probing is accordingly a representation-selection problem: beyond fitting a classifier, one must choose a subspace that preserves the intended behavioral feature and excludes spurious correlation.

## Appendix B LLM Judge Prompt

We use GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025) to interpret directions.

You are interpreting a principal component direction in a neural representation space.
This direction is bipolar:

- Positive activations mean movement toward one pole.

- Negative activations mean movement toward the opposite pole.

- Larger magnitudes mean a stronger match to that pole.

Each line is formatted as token<TAB>activation, with activations normalized to integers from -10 to +10.

The examples below were selected from a dataset with this setup: The model is instructed to Roleplay in a simple scenario.
The model is asked a question which gives a strategic chance to lie.

High-positive examples:

{positive_examples}

High-negative examples:

{negative_examples}

Infer the dominant contrast captured by the direction using both the positive and negative examples.

Important instructions:

# Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection

Daniel Yoo

  
Adrians Skapars

###### Abstract

For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes evaluated on 3 held-out datasets, source-trained probes restricted to a small subset of source-domain principal components (PCs) nearly match target-trained probes. An LLM judge's OOD scores over PC interpretations, computed without target data, select a subspace that closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging.

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Linear probes (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019) are unreliable out-of-distribution (Kirch et al., 2026) despite linear representation of behavioral concepts (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Park et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025), and pick up spurious correlations (Orgad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). We work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than the model's latent dimensions; cf. Mu et al. (2018), where removing top PCs of an embedding space helps downstream tasks, and Kantamneni et al. (2025), who use top-PC projections as a probe baseline. Question: which PC subsets support generalizable probe training, and how are they identified?

Testbed: deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), source Roleplaying, targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025).

Contributions:

•

Section 4.2: target-guided greedy search finds 8–15 source PCs on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe.

•

Section 4.3: rankings by source-probe or target-probe weights do not transfer better than the full-representation baseline.

•

Section 4.5: an LLM judge partially recovers the subspace without target data.

Figure 1: Overview of PC-based subspace selection for OOD deception probing. Activations are projected onto the source-domain PCA basis, candidate PC directions are filtered, and probes are trained on the selected low-dimensional subspace.

## 2 Related Work

#### Linear concept directions in activation space.

Linear true/false structure across datasets (Marks and Tegmark, 2024); the linear representation hypothesis linking probing and steering (Park et al., 2024); population-level directions for honesty and emotion (Zou et al., 2025). A single refusal direction (Arditi et al., 2024); an “assistant” axis (Lu et al., 2026).

#### Linear probes and their limitations.

Probing as analysis (Alain and Bengio, 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019); safety-relevant probes for latent truthfulness (Burns et al., 2024) and strategic deception (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Critiques: probe accuracy versus encoded information (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Ravichander et al., 2021); uneven OOD generalization of strong in-distribution probes (kramár2026buildingproductionreadyprobesgemini).

#### Interpreting features with natural-language explanations.

LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al., 2023), extended to SAE features ((Paulo et al., 2025), (Bricken et al., 2023)); concept ablation during fine-tuning via automated interpretation (Casademunt et al., 2025).

## 3 Setup

#### Datasets.

4 datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) (Appendix A): Roleplaying (source); Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (targets). GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) labels: honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); -1 removed.

#### Language models.

Layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), the highest cross-domain AUROC layer in Ying et al. (2026); mean over assistant-response tokens.

#### Probe training and evaluation.

Source activations are standardized; targets use source statistics. PCA on scaled source activations, top 100 PCs retained. Logistic regression ( $\lambda=10$ ); for subset $S$, activations projected onto $S$; baseline on full standardized activations. The top 100 are used since SAE decoder alignment (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index (Appendix C); no claim is made that low-index PCs generalize better.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Setting a baseline

Figure 2: Probe AUROC on target datasets for source-trained probes on full representations (blue) and top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Error bars: 95% CIs

Source-trained full-representation baseline AUROC: 0.874 (Insider Trading Confirm), 0.706 (Insider Trading Report), 0.606 (Sandbagging). Target-trained, top-100 source PCs, 5-fold CV: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869.

### 4.2 Showing a transferable subspace exists

Figure 3: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the full-representation baseline (blue), top-k PCs by variance (teal, k matched to greedy), and greedy oracle PCs (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Greedy oracle: from an empty set, add the PC among the top 100 maximizing target AUROC of a probe fit on source projections onto the current subset; stop when gain $\le$ 0.001. 5-fold CV over the target: selection on non-held-out folds, evaluation on the held-out fold. Mean subset size: 15 (Insider Trading Report), 8 (Insider Trading Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Being target-guided, it is an upper bound, not an unbiased OOD estimate. Control: top $k$ PCs by variance, $k$ matched to greedy.

Greedy nearly matches target-trained probes on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging, +0.22 and +0.23 AUROC over baseline. Variance control matches greedy only on Insider Trading Confirm and falls far behind on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

### 4.3 Testing hypotheses for transferable principal components

Figure 4: Probe AUROC across the three targets for three PC-selection rules: ranking by source-probe weights (red), by target-probe weights (pink), and greedy oracle selection (purple). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Hypotheses: greedy PCs are (i) those individually separating target classes, or (ii) those the source probe weights most. Rankings by $|w_j|\,\sigma_j$ from a probe on source-PCA projections fit on source data (‘source-PCA probe’) or target data (‘target-PCA probe’); in both cases a probe is then trained on source data projected onto the top $k$ ranked PCs. $k$ from greedy on the full target (no CV): $k=13$ for Insider Trading Report, 7 for Insider Trading Confirm, 14 for Sandbagging; greedy numbers therefore differ slightly from Section 4.2.

Source-PCA probe ≈ full-representation baseline. Target-PCA probe: good on Insider Trading Report, below greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, below chance on Sandbagging. See Appendix D.

### 4.4 Interpreting the transferable subspace

Following Bills et al. (2023) and Casademunt et al. (2025): for each of the top 100 source PCs, the 8 most and 8 least activating source examples are given to an LLM, which describes positive pole, negative pole, and direction, and assigns an OOD score on 1–10 (Appendix B). Maximum observed score: 6. PCs scoring 6 in both runs: 19.

5 PCs appear in greedy selections for more than one target; 3 of 5 score 6. Of the top 5 source-PCA-probe PCs, 1 scores 6. Appendix E.

### 4.5 Selecting a subspace by interpreting PCs

Figure 5: Probe AUROC across the three targets for the interp-selected subspace (red; 19 PCs) versus three controls: full-representation baseline (blue), top-19 PCs by variance (teal), and the remaining 81 PCs after ablating the interp-selected PCs (brown). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Probe on the 19 interp-selected PCs (score 6 in both of two runs), no target data. Controls: the 81 ablated-complement PCs; top 19 by variance.

Interp-selected beats baseline on all 3 targets, beats the variance control (by wide margins on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging), and beats the 81-PC ablation on all 3. With gap closed $=(\text{AUROC}_{\text{interp}}-\text{AUROC}_{\text{base}})/(\text{AUROC}_{\text{greedy}}-\text{AUROC}_{\text{base}})$: Insider Trading Report 78% (baseline 0.706, greedy 0.929); Sandbagging 25% (greedy 0.832). Insider Trading Confirm: baseline near ceiling, all methods but interp-ablated roughly equal; uninformative.

## 5 Limitations

Single model and source dataset.
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15; source Roleplaying (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Insider Trading Confirm baseline is already 0.874. Other model families and datasets untested.

Sandbagging margins are small.
0.606 to 0.662, 25% of the gap to greedy (0.832); Sandbagging is the most out-of-distribution target. Insider Trading Report: 0.706 to 0.881, 78% of the gap to 0.929.

Linear pipeline. PCA projection plus logistic regression throughout; nonlinear probes and other readout locations untested.

No causal validation.
PC “encodings” rest on top-activating examples and judge verbalizations; no inference-time ablation of high-scoring PCs.

## 6 Conclusion

A small subset of source PCs supports cross-domain transfer of deception probes nearly matching target-trained probes, is not recovered by source-side or target-side separability, and is partially recovered by LLM-judge OOD scores without target data. OOD probing is thus a representation-selection problem: choose a subspace preserving the behavioral feature and excluding spurious correlation, in addition to fitting a classifier.

## Appendix B LLM Judge Prompt

Judge: GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025).

You are interpreting a principal component direction in a neural representation space.
This direction is bipolar:

- Positive activations mean movement toward one pole.

- Negative activations mean movement toward the opposite pole.

- Larger magnitudes mean a stronger match to that pole.

Each line is formatted as token<TAB>activation, with activations normalized to integers from -10 to +10.

The examples below were selected from a dataset with this setup: The model is instructed to Roleplay in a simple scenario.
The model is asked a question which gives a strategic chance to lie.

High-positive examples:

{positive_examples}

High-negative examples:

{negative_examples}

Infer the dominant contrast captured by the direction using both the positive and negative examples.

Important instructions:

- Do not assume the direction is a broad sentiment direction unless the examples clearly support that.

- Prefer the narrowest accurate description over a broad generic one.

- Do not overgeneralize beyond what is supported by the examples.

- Rate how likely this direction is to be useful for out-of-distribution deception on a scale from 1 to 10, and briefly explain why.

- Give low scores to directions that are mainly surface cues, lexical habits, or task-specific phrasing, even if they correlate with deception in these examples.

- A direction that is noisy, brittle, context-dependent, or likely to fail under different wording or domains should usually be scored around 1 to 4, not 5 or above.

- Reserve scores of 5 or higher for directions that seem plausibly tied to a more general deception-relevant strategy or behavior, rather than local wording.

Write your answer in exactly this format:

Positive pole: ...

Negative pole: ...

Shared direction: ...

OOD deception usefulness (1-10): ...

ANSWER Q4: This is not established and should not be assumed. The target-PCA ranking used the target data without an out-of-sample selection evaluation, so its good Report result may partly reflect target-data overfitting and is not an unbiased estimate for fresh examples.

ANSWER Q5: Yes, nominally, but not clearly or meaningfully. The paper says interp-selection beats the baseline on all three targets, while noting that on Insider Trading Confirm the baseline and nearly all non-ablated methods are roughly equal.

ANSWER Q6: Not settled. Greedy search is a heuristic that finds one high-performing set and does not test alternative, redundant, or equally transferable PC subsets, so uniqueness is not demonstrated.

ANSWER Q7: Section 4.4’s main evidence would disappear. Its evidence is that five PCs recur across target-specific greedy sets and three of those receive the maximum judge score; with no shared Sandbagging PCs, there would be no such multi-target enrichment.

ANSWER Q8: No. The paper states that on Insider Trading Confirm all methods except the interp-ablated control are roughly equal, so interp-selection does not clearly beat the top-19-by-variance control.

ANSWER Q9: The full-representation baseline is already 0.874 AUROC, compared with 0.936 for a target-trained probe, leaving only a 0.062 gap and limited room for differentiation. Consequently, nearly all selection methods cluster near the ceiling.

ANSWER Q10: No. Target-weight ranking performs well on Insider Trading Report, falls below greedy on Insider Trading Confirm, and is below chance on Sandbagging, showing severe target-dependent unreliability.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. The paper only reports enrichment at the maximum observed score of 6 and evaluates a threshold-selected 19-PC set; it does not measure transfer performance systematically across judge scores 1–6 or establish a reliable monotonic relationship.

ANSWER Q13: The judge can assign low scores to genuinely useful PCs and therefore omit them. For example, PC9 appears in the greedy Report and Sandbagging sets but receives an OOD score of 3, so the score-6 interp-selection rule misses at least one empirically transferable direction.

ANSWER Q14: Not settled. Layer 15 was chosen because prior work found it had the highest cross-domain AUROC, but this paper tests PC subspace selection only at that layer and does not compare layers for this method.

ANSWER Q15: PC62 and PC57 are the strongest candidates, followed by PC86. PC62 and PC57 are greedily selected for both Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging and score 6, while PC86 is selected for both Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging and also scores 6; these recommendations remain specific to this model and PCA basis.

ANSWER Q16: It would undermine Section 4.3’s finding that source-probe-weight rankings perform only near the baseline and the conclusion that transferable subspaces are not recovered by source-side separability. ANSWER Q17: They should choose the 19-PC interp-selected probe. It beats the full-representation baseline on all three targets, whereas ranking by source-probe weights performs approximately like the baseline.

ANSWER Q18: Insider Trading Report has only 61 deceptive retained examples versus 194 honest examples, so AUROC gains estimated on non-held-out folds can be noisy. Adaptively searching up to 100 PCs and accepting gains as small as 0.001 creates substantial multiple-selection overfitting risk, making the target-guided oracle optimistic.
